Contextual Decision Making: Predictive or Generative

L. Jeff Hong    Weihuan Huang    Xinyao Li
Abstract

Contextual decision making uses observed covariates to guide decisions under uncertainty. Two natural approaches are predict-then-optimize (PtO), which learns the conditional expected objective, and generate-then-optimize (GtO), which learns conditional uncertainty and optimizes using generated scenarios. We study when each approach is preferable by examining how the choice of learning target affects statistical accuracy and optimization tractability. Although PtO learns a narrower target, our regret bounds show how differences in smoothness can offset GtO’s additional dimensional burden. Exploiting smoothness also raises an optimization tradeoff: within the class of nonnegative-weight PtO methods studied, a lower bound limits the gains from additional smoothness, while more flexible methods may introduce signed weights and lose the guarantee of preserving convexity. GtO preserves scenario-wise convexity, but requires learning a richer object and generating scenarios for optimization. Synthetic experiments and a real case study illustrate how these tradeoffs vary with data availability and problem structure. Together with the scope for reusing a model across tasks, our findings provide practical guidance for choosing between the approaches without identifying a universal winner.

keywords
contextual stochastic optimization; predict-then-optimize; generate-then-optimize; conditional generative models; statistical efficiency; convexity preservation.

1 Introduction

Modern operating environments provide decision makers with rich contextual information. Retailers observe promotions, recent sales, and local market conditions before replenishing inventory. Logistics providers use congestion and demand signals to plan deliveries and reserve capacity. Service systems use workload forecasts and current operating conditions to make staffing decisions, as illustrated by feature-based approaches to hospital nurse staffing (Ban and Rudin 2019). Healthcare providers use patient characteristics and clinical information to personalize treatment and allocate care resources (Shen et al. 2021). In each setting, the challenge is to turn information available before a decision into an effective response to an uncertain outcome. Contextual stochastic optimization (CSO) provides a framework for doing so by minimizing expected cost conditional on the observed context (Bertsimas and Kallus 2020, Sadana et al. 2025).

Let XX denote the context, YY the uncertain outcome, zz the decision, and c⁡(z,x,y)c(z;x,y) the cost. After observing X=x0X=x_{0}, the decision maker seeks to minimize the conditional expected objective

h⁡(z,x0)=𝔼⁡[c⁡(z,X,Y)∣X=x0].h(z;x_{0})=\mathbb{E}[c(z;X,Y)\mid X=x_{0}].

We focus on convex CSO: the feasible decision set is convex, and the cost is convex in zz for each context and outcome. The conditional expected objective is consequently convex as well. The difficulty is that this objective is unknown and must be learned from historical observations of contexts and outcomes.

Two approaches arise naturally. A predictive approach learns the conditional expected objective and optimizes the fitted objective when a new context is observed (Bertsimas and Kallus 2020). We refer to this approach as Predict-then-Optimize (PtO). A generative approach learns the conditional distribution of YY given XX, generates scenarios for the observed context, and optimizes their average cost (Gong et al. 2024). We refer to this approach as Generate-then-Optimize (GtO). For instance, in a retail inventory problem, PtO estimates expected inventory cost, whereas GtO generates demand scenarios under which inventory decisions can be evaluated. PtO concentrates learning on the objective of interest. GtO learns a conditional distribution that can support different objectives involving the same uncertain outcome.

The rise of generative AI makes the generative approach increasingly appealing. Advances in generative modeling provide flexible tools for learning conditional distributions and producing scenarios (Bond-Taylor et al. 2022, Yang et al. 2024). Further progress may make these tools easier to develop and use, while creating opportunities to incorporate qualitative context, such as descriptions of operating conditions or expert judgments expressed in language. As these capabilities develop, more organizations may be able to use generative models in operational decision making. Yet the ability to generate realistic scenarios does not by itself establish that learning a conditional distribution is preferable to learning the expected objective. The choice still depends on the data available, the optimization problem to be solved, and the decisions the model is intended to support.

This motivates our central question: When should contextual decision making be predictive, and when should it be generative? Both approaches can be applied to many of the same decision problems, but their relative appeal is not immediately clear. Learning the expected objective focuses on what a particular task requires, while learning the conditional distribution provides scenarios that can be used to evaluate decisions. We seek to understand when each approach is useful and to develop practical guidance for choosing between them. As generative AI makes scenario generation more accessible, this choice will become increasingly important.

The first consideration is statistical: how difficult is it to learn the expected objective or the conditional distribution from the available data? PtO avoids estimating how probability is distributed across outcomes, which can be valuable when data are limited or the uncertain outcome is high-dimensional. GtO must account for both the context and the uncertain outcome when learning the conditional distribution. Dimension alone, however, does not determine the difficulty of learning. Smoothness also matters because it allows observations at nearby contexts to inform one another, a central principle in nonparametric regression and conditional-density estimation (Stone 1982, Li et al. 2022). The conditional distribution may vary smoothly with the context even when the expected objective changes abruptly because costs depend on thresholds or operating rules. Learning the expected objective can therefore involve fewer dimensions without necessarily being easier.

We examine this tradeoff through bounds on regret, defined as the excess expected cost relative to an optimal decision. For PtO, our bound for kernel ridge regression (KRR) describes how greater objective smoothness can mitigate the effect of context dimension. For GtO, the corresponding analysis accounts for the dimension and smoothness of the conditional distribution, with conditional diffusion models providing a concrete instance (Fu et al. 2024). These results suggest assessing dimension and smoothness together when choosing an approach. PtO is attractive when the expected objective is sufficiently smooth to be learned accurately from the available data. GtO becomes more attractive when the conditional distribution is easier to learn because its greater smoothness compensates for the additional outcome dimension. The bounds explain these competing effects and inform the choice.

The second consideration is computational: how does learning affect the optimization problem that must ultimately be solved? Although the original decision problem is convex, an approximation learned from data need not preserve that property. A broad class of PtO methods fits the expected objective as a weighted sum of observed costs,

h^n​(z,x)=∑i=1nωn,i​(x)​c​(z,xi,yi),\hat{h}_{n}(z;x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{n,i}(x)c(z;x_{i},y_{i}),

where {(xi,yi)}i=1n\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} are historical observations (Bertsimas and Kallus 2020, Bertsimas and Koduri 2022). Nonnegative weights preserve convexity. Methods such as KRR can exploit higher-order smoothness but may assign negative weights, so their fitted objectives are no longer guaranteed to be convex. GtO preserves convexity by averaging scenario costs with equal positive weights, but must generate the scenarios and solve the resulting sample average approximation (SAA) problem (Shapiro et al. 2009). The choice of learning method thus affects both statistical accuracy and the computation needed to obtain a decision.

Our analysis makes this connection precise. For the class of nonnegative, covariate-based PtO weighting rules considered, we establish a lower bound of order n−4/(dx+4)n^{-4/(d_{x}+4)} on worst-case expected regret, where dxd_{x} is the context dimension. The bound holds even for arbitrarily smooth objectives in the constructed problem class. Within this class, the nonnegative weights that preserve convexity limit the benefit that additional smoothness can provide. KRR can benefit from higher-order smoothness, but its negative weights may complicate optimization. The extent of that difficulty depends on the cost function: negative weights do not invariably produce a nonconvex or difficult problem. A predictive method should therefore be assessed together with the optimization problem induced by its fitted objective.

For GtO, our regret bound separates the error in learning the conditional distribution from the error caused by using finitely many generated scenarios. Under the stated assumptions, the bound consists of a term proportional to the conditional-distribution learning error and an SAA term of order m−1/2m^{-1/2}, where mm is the number of generated scenarios. Improving the learned distribution reduces the first error, whereas generating more scenarios reduces the second at additional computational cost. Preserving convexity therefore does not by itself imply faster decisions. PtO is attractive when its fitted objective remains easy to optimize and rapid responses are important. GtO is attractive when retaining the convex structure is valuable and the time available permits scenario generation and optimization. This distinction is particularly relevant when decisions must be made repeatedly under tight response-time requirements.

The third consideration is how broadly the learned model will be used. A model serving one objective can concentrate its learning effort on that task. In practice, however, several operational teams may face the same conditional distribution while making decisions with different objectives or constraints. When data analysis and operations reside in different departments, adapting a model to each objective can also require substantial coordination. GtO offers one way to organize this work: a data team develops a common generative model, and operational teams use its scenarios in their own decision problems. PtO can also support reuse through shared weights, features, or estimated objective components. The relevant question is how much adaptation and coordination each additional use requires. A stable, specialized task makes objective learning appealing, whereas a range of tasks sharing the same conditional distribution increases the value of a reusable generative model. The latter may be worth developing even when it offers no advantage for an individual task.

Taken together, these three considerations provide practical guidance on choosing between PtO and GtO. The choice involves balancing what can be learned reliably, what can be optimized within the available time, and how the model will serve the organization’s decisions. Neither approach is preferred in all settings, and an advantage along one of these dimensions may be offset by a disadvantage along another. We draw on the theoretical results and these practical considerations to develop rules of thumb that help decision makers assess that balance.

We use two numerical examples, a contextual newsvendor problem and a product placement problem, to examine the tradeoffs and provide evidence supporting this guidance. We then extend the comparison through a real case study of fresh-retail inventory using operational data from a retail chain. With both continuous and categorical features, this case goes beyond the setting of our theoretical analysis and provides further evidence of the usefulness of our managerial insights in practice.

1.1 Related Literature

Our work builds on contextual stochastic optimization, where historical data and contextual information are used to improve decisions under uncertainty. Hannah et al. (2010) study nonparametric methods for stochastic optimization with observable state information. Ban and Rudin (2019) develop feature-based methods for the newsvendor problem, and Bertsimas and Kallus (2020) provide a general prescriptive analytics framework using side information. Bertsimas and Koduri (2022) develop methods based on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, while Bertsimas et al. (2023) extend optimization with side information to dynamic settings. Sadana et al. (2025) review the broader literature. The weighting frameworks of Bertsimas and Kallus (2020) and Bertsimas and Koduri (2022) provide the foundation for our PtO analysis. We use this representation to examine how the choice between objective learning and conditional-distribution learning affects statistical performance and downstream optimization.

A related stream of research studies how training can account for the decisions that a learned model will support. Donti et al. (2017) incorporate optimization into task-based and decision-focused learning, while Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022) develop the Smart Predict-then-Optimize framework and the SPO+ surrogate loss. Broader accounts are provided by Mandi et al. (2024) and Sadana et al. (2025). In this paper, PtO refers specifically to learning the conditional expected objective; elsewhere, the term also describes predicting inputs to an optimization model. Our comparison concerns what is learned, while decision-focused training concerns how learning is aligned with decision quality. These questions are complementary, since either an objective model or a generative model can, in principle, be trained using decision-focused criteria. We study the choice of learning target within a framework that separates learning from optimization.

The statistical foundations of our comparison come from nonparametric regression and conditional-density estimation, where smoothness and dimension govern estimation difficulty (Stone 1982, Li et al. 2022). Generative models provide practical methods for learning distributions, including variational autoencoders, adversarial models, normalizing flows, and diffusion models; Bond-Taylor et al. (2022) and Yang et al. (2024) provide reviews. Our conditional-diffusion analysis uses the learning guarantees of Fu et al. (2024), and our retail implementation uses TabCSDI (Zheng and Charoenphakdee 2022). We use these existing methods to study the decision consequences of learning a conditional distribution.

The use of generated scenarios also connects our work to stochastic programming. Scenario construction and reduction have long been used to approximate stochastic optimization problems (Høyland and Wallace 2001, Dupačová et al. 2003). Recent studies use deep generative models to construct decision-relevant scenarios or incorporate optimization objectives into generative training (Pisinger and Hemmati Golsefidi 2026, Wang et al. 2026, Zhao et al. 2026). Our contribution is a comparative analysis of PtO and GtO that connects regret guarantees with preservation of optimization structure and computational requirements. This analysis supports practical guidance for choosing between the approaches and complements research on improving the performance of either one.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formulates the problem and performance criteria. Section 3 analyzes weighted PtO methods, and Section 4 develops the GtO regret analysis. Section 5 draws practical guidance from the comparison. Section 6 presents the numerical and empirical studies, and Section 7 concludes. The appendix contains the proofs, implementation details, and supplementary numerical results.

2 Problem Formulation

We consider a convex contextual stochastic optimization (CSO) problem of the form

z∗(x)∈argminz∈𝒵{h(z;x):=𝔼[c(z;X,Y)|X=x]},z^{\ast}(x)\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\Big\{h(z;x):=\E\big[c(z;X,Y)\,|\,X=x\big]\Big\}, (1)

where XX is a random vector of covariates taking values in 𝒳⊆ℝdx\mathcal{X}\subseteq\R^{d_{x}}, YY is a vector of uncertain parameters taking values in 𝒴⊆ℝdy\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\R^{d_{y}} and potentially correlated with XX, zz is the vector of decision variables with the feasible set 𝒵⊆ℝdz\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\R^{d_{z}}, and c⁡(z,x,y)c(z;x,y) is a given cost function that is convex in the decision variable zz. In the offline stage, we have access only to historical data 𝒟n={(xi,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{n}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}, consisting of nn observations of (X,Y)(X,Y). In the online stage, upon observing a new covariate realization X=x0X=x_{0}, we make an online decision z∗​(x0)z^{\ast}(x_{0}) via solving Problem (1). We assume that the offline observations {(xi,yi)}i=1n\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} are independent and identical distributed (i.i.d.) copies of (X,Y)(X,Y), and that the online covariate X=x0X=x_{0} observed at the decision epoch is an independent draw from the same distribution as the training covariates. We impose the following structural assumptions on the feasible set and the cost function.

{assumption}

The feasible set 𝒵⊂ℝdz\mathcal{Z}\subset\R^{d_{z}} is nonempty, convex, and compact. We denote its diameter by diam(𝒵):=sup{∥z1−z2∥:z1,z2∈𝒵}=D<∞.\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{Z}):=\sup\{\|z_{1}-z_{2}\|:z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathcal{Z}\}=D<\infty. For every (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, the cost function c⁡(⋅,x,y)c(\cdot;x,y) is convex on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, uniformly Lipschitz with respect to zz, i.e., there exists a constant G<∞G<\infty such that for all z1,z2∈𝒵z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathcal{Z} and all (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, we have |c⁡(z2,x,y)−c⁡(z1,x,y)|≤G​‖z2−z1‖,|c(z_{2};x,y)-c(z_{1};x,y)|\leq G\|z_{2}-z_{1}\|, and uniformly bounded, i.e., there exists a constant M<∞M<\infty such that for all z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} and (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, we have |c⁡(z,x,y)|≤M.|c(z;x,y)|\leq M.

The assumptions for the feasible set in Assumption 2 is standard in stochastic programming and contextual stochastic optimization to guarantee the existence of minimizers, see, e.g., Shapiro et al. (2009), Bertsimas and Kallus (2020), Bertsimas and Koduri (2022). The convexity assumption for the cost function in Assumption 2 restricts our focus for the convex CSO problem. Assumption 2 also imposes a uniform Lipschitz and bounded condition on the cost function; such conditions are reasonable technical assumptions and used in the literature of contextual stochastic optimization, see, e.g., Bertsimas and Kallus (2020), Bertsimas and Koduri (2022).

Under Assumption 2, the conditional objective h⁡(⋅,x)h(\cdot;x) is convex for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, uniformly GG-Lipschitz continuous in zz over x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, and uniformly bounded. Consequently, h⁡(⋅,x)h(\cdot;x) is continuous on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Since 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is compact, the set of optimal solutions in Problem (1) is nonempty, compact, and convex for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}. We do not require the optimal solution to be unique. Moreover, we impose the following regularity conditions on the conditional objective and the covariate distribution.

{assumption}

There exists a constant Lh<∞L_{h}<\infty such that h⁡(z,x):=𝔼⁡[c⁡(z,X,Y)|X=x]h(z;x):=\mathbb{E}[c(z;X,Y)|X=x] is LhL_{h}-Lipschitz in xx, uniformly in zz, i.e., |h⁡(z,x)−h⁡(z,x′)|≤Lh​‖x−x′‖|h(z;x)-h(z;x^{\prime})|\leq L_{h}\|x-x^{\prime}\| holds for all z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} and for all x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}.

{assumption}

The covariates are supported on the hypercube 𝒳=[0,1]dx\mathcal{X}=[0,1]^{d_{x}} and admit a density pp with respect to the Lebesgue measure satisfying 0<pmin≤p⁡(x)≤pmax<∞0<p_{\min}\leq p(x)\leq p_{\max}<\infty for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}.

For a data-driven decision rule z^n​(x0)\hat{z}_{n}(x_{0}) constructed from 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}, we evaluate its performance through the conditional optimality gap (regret)

ℛn​(x0):=h⁡(z^n​(x0),x0)−h⁡(z∗​(x0),x0),\mathcal{R}_{n}(x_{0}):=h\left(\hat{z}_{n}(x_{0});x_{0}\right)-h\left(z^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0}\right),

and, when appropriate, its expected counterpart ℛn:=𝔼X⁡[h⁡(z^n​(X),X)−h⁡(z∗​(X),X)].\mathcal{R}_{n}:=\E_{X}[h(\hat{z}_{n}(X);X)-h(z^{*}(X);X)]. For ease of interpretation and comparison across problem instances, we also consider a normalized performance measure based on the regret. Let z^B​(x)\hat{z}_{\mathrm{B}}(x) denote a benchmark decision rule and define its expected regret by ℛB:=𝔼X⁡[h⁡(z^B​(X),X)−h⁡(z∗​(X),X)].\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{B}}:=\E_{X}[h(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{B}}(X);X)-h(z^{\ast}(X);X)]. Provided that ℛB>0\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{B}}>0, we define the relative cost of z^n\hat{z}_{n} as

RCn:=1−ℛnℛB=𝔼X⁡[h⁡(z^B​(X),X)]−𝔼X⁡[h⁡(z^n​(X),X)]𝔼X⁡[h⁡(z^B​(X),X)]−𝔼X⁡[h⁡(z∗​(X),X)].\mathrm{RC}_{n}:=1-\frac{\mathcal{R}_{n}}{\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{B}}}\,=\,\frac{\E_{X}[h(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{B}}(X);X)]-\E_{X}[h(\hat{z}_{n}(X);X)]}{\E_{X}[h(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{B}}(X);X)]-\E_{X}[h(z^{\ast}(X);X)]}. (2)

Thus, the relative cost measures the fraction of the benchmark’s optimality gap eliminated by the data-driven decision rule: RCn=0\mathrm{RC}_{n}=0 indicates performance identical to the benchmark, whereas RCn=1\mathrm{RC}_{n}=1 corresponds to the optimal decision. A value of RC\mathrm{RC} closer to 11 indicates that the decision rule performs better than the benchmark, while a negative value of RC\mathrm{RC} indicates that the decision rule performs worse than the benchmark. In the numerical experiments, we use an unconditional SAA — an SAA method for Problem (1) without the condition {X=x0}\{X=x_{0}\} — as the benchmark and an oracle solution as the proxy for the optimal decision, yielding the equivalent empirical definition reported in Section 6. This relative-cost measure has been widely used as a normalized performance metric for evaluating data-driven decision rules in Problem (1); see, e.g., Bertsimas and Kallus (2020) and Bertsimas and Koduri (2022).

Let FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) denote the conditional distribution function of YY given X=xX=x. The conditional objective can then be written as

h⁡(z,x)=∫𝒴c⁡(z,x,y)​d​FY|X​(y|x).h(z;x)=\int_{\mathcal{Y}}c(z;x,y)\,\mathrm{d}F_{Y|X}(y|x).

Thus, the conditional distribution FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) determines the stochastic information relevant to the decision problem, while data-driven methods may extract and utilize this information at different levels. In particular, one may directly estimate the induced conditional objective h⁡(z,x)h(z;x), or instead learn the underlying conditional distribution FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) and subsequently construct the objective through generated samples.

These two strategies give rise to two broad paradigms for contextual decision making: a predictive approach, which learns the conditional objective h⁡(z,x)h(z;x) and then optimizes it, and a generative approach, which learns the conditional distribution FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) (or a conditional simulator) and then optimizes using generated scenarios. This distinction raises a fundamental question: How should we choose between the two paradigms? In general, neither is uniformly preferable. Their relative pros and cons depend on both the statistical structure of the underlying problem and the computational properties of the resulting optimization problem. Accordingly, in the following sections, we study the predictive and generative paradigms separately and compare them along two central dimensions: convexity preservation, which concerns whether the learned representation preserves convexity that facilitate the downstream optimization, and statistical efficiency, which concerns how effectively each paradigm exploits the available offline data. Our analysis is intended to identify the problem characteristics under which each paradigm is particularly well suited and thereby provide insightful guidance on the choice between predictive and generative approaches.

3 Predict-then-Optimize

Predict-then-optimize (PtO) is a widely used framework for contextual stochastic optimization (Bertsimas and Kallus 2020, Bertsimas and Koduri 2022, Sadana et al. 2025). Under this paradigm, the conditional objective function hh is first estimated from historical data 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} and then optimized for a realized covariate x0x_{0}. Most PtO methods approximate the conditional objective using a weighted empirical average of the observed costs. Specifically, the estimated objective takes the form

h^n​(z,x):=∑i=1nωn,i​(x)​c​(z,xi,yi),\hat{h}_{n}(z;x):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{n,i}(x)\,c(z;x_{i},y_{i}), (3)

where the weights ωn,i​(x0)\omega_{n,i}(x_{0}) are determined by the statistical procedure used to estimate the conditional expectation h⁡(z,x)h(z;x), and the decision rule is obtained by solving z^n​(x0)∈arg⁡minz∈𝒵​h^n​(z,x0)\hat{z}_{n}(x_{0})\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\hat{h}_{n}(z;x_{0}).

The estimator in Equation (3) is linear in the observed responses and encompasses a broad class of classical regression methods, both parametric and nonparametric. Examples include ordinary least squares and ridge regression on the parametric side (Hastie et al. 2009), and kk-nearest-neighbor regression, kernel and local polynomial regression, smoothing splines, and kernel ridge regression on the nonparametric side (Wahba 1990, Hastie et al. 2009). Within this broad class, we focus on nonparametric methods and, following Bertsimas and Koduri (2022), distinguish between local and global methods.

3.1 Local Methods: Convexity Preservation at the Cost of Statistical Efficiency

Traditional local approximation methods, such as kk-nearest neighbors, Nadaraya–Watson kernel smoothing, local averaging, classification and regression trees, and random forests, determines the weights ωn,i​(x0)\omega_{n,i}(x_{0}) according to the proximity between the historical covariates xix_{i} and the realized covariate x0x_{0}; see Wahba (1990), Hastie et al. (2009). They estimate the conditional objective primarily by pooling information from observations that are locally relevant to x0x_{0}. Many commonly used local methods naturally generate nonnegative weights. Some exceptions, such as local linear methods, may produce signed weights, but can be modified to enforce nonnegativity (Bertsimas and Kallus 2020). From an optimization perspective, the property of nonnegative weights is important because it preserves the convexity of estimated objective h^​(⋅,x0)\hat{h}(\cdot;x_{0}) whenever the cost c⁡(⋅,x,y)c(\cdot;x,y) is convex.

Although local methods therefore preserve convexity of the downstream optimization problem, their statistical efficiency is inherently limited by the curse of dimensionality. These methods rely on locality, assigning substantial weights only to observations close to x0x_{0}. As the covariate dimension increases, observations become increasingly sparse in local neighborhoods, making accurate local estimation progressively more difficult. For example, the PtO formulation based on Nadaraya–Watson kernel smoothing estimation with a spherical kernel achieves a decision regret rate of

𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[h⁡(z^n​(X),X)−h⁡(z∗​(X),X)∣𝒟n]]=𝒪~​(n−1dx+2),\E\Big[\E\big[h(\hat{z}_{n}(X);X)-h(z^{*}(X);X)\mid\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big]\,=\,\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(n^{-\frac{1}{d_{x}+2}}\right),

which deteriorates as the covariate dimension dxd_{x} increases; see Wang et al. (2024).

The curse of dimensionality underlying local methods can be understood through the usual bias–variance tradeoff. In high-dimensional covariate spaces, a small neighborhood around x0x_{0} typically contains few observations, leading to high variance in the estimated conditional objective. Enlarging the neighborhood increases the effective sample size and reduces variance, but at the cost of incorporating observations farther from x0x_{0}, thereby increasing approximation bias when the conditional objective varies with the covariates. As dxd_{x} increases, balancing these two sources of error becomes progressively more difficult, which leads to slower estimation of h⁡(z,x0)h(z;x_{0}) and, consequently, slower convergence of the resulting decision regret.

3.2 Global Methods: Statistical Efficiency at the Cost of Convexity Preservation

To improve performance in high-dimensional settings, global regression methods based on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) have been employed (Bertsimas and Koduri 2022). Unlike local methods, RKHS-based approaches determine the weights by solving a regularized optimization problem over a function space, which leads to a kernel ridge regression (KRR) estimator under squared loss. Specifically, for each fixed z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} and a given kernel function KK, KRR estimates h⁡(z,⋅)h(z;\cdot) by

h^n​(z,⋅)∈arg⁡minf∈ℋ​{1n​∑i=1n(f⁡(xi)−c⁡(z,xi,yi))2+λn​‖f‖ℋ2},\hat{h}_{n}(z;\cdot)\in\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal{H}}\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(f(x_{i})-c(z;x_{i},y_{i})\big)^{2}+\lambda_{n}\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\right\},

where λn>0\lambda_{n}>0 is the regularization parameter and ℋ\mathcal{H} is the RKHS induced by the kernel function KK. By the representer theorem (Wahba 1990, Schölkopf et al. 2001), the resulting estimator can be written as

h^n​(z,x0)=∑i=1nωn,iKRR​(x0)​c​(z,xi,yi),\hat{h}_{n}(z;x_{0})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega^{\mathrm{KRR}}_{n,i}(x_{0})c(z;x_{i},y_{i}), (4)

where the KRR weights ωnKRR​(x0)=(Kn+n​λn​In)−1​kn​(x0)\omega^{\mathrm{KRR}}_{n}(x_{0})=(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}k_{n}(x_{0}), Kn=(K⁡(xi,xj))i,j=1nK_{n}=(K(x_{i},x_{j}))_{i,j=1}^{n}, and kn​(x0)=(K⁡(x1,x0),…,K⁡(xn,x0))⊤k_{n}(x_{0})=(K(x_{1},x_{0}),\ldots,K(x_{n},x_{0}))^{\top}. Thus, λn\lambda_{n} controls the tradeoff between goodness of fit and regularization, while the resulting KRR weights are generally not restricted to be nonnegative.

This global approach allows the estimator to exploit information from the entire training sample rather than only observations in a local neighborhood. Consequently, it can leverage the smoothness of the conditional objective h⁡(z,⋅)h(z;\cdot) with respect to the covariates xx for each fixed decision zz. When h⁡(z,⋅)h(z;\cdot) exhibits sufficiently high-order smoothness, RKHS-based methods can translate this regularity into faster convergence rates with substantially weaker dependence on the covariate dimension dxd_{x} than local methods.

We instantiate the RKHS approach using the Matérn kernel K=KνK=K_{\nu} with smoothness parameter ν>0\nu>0, and set s:=ν+dx/2s:=\nu+d_{x}/2. To express the smoothness condition in terms of classical derivatives, we restrict attention to values of ν\nu for which ss is an integer. It is well known that the RKHS ℋν\mathcal{H}_{\nu} induced by KνK_{\nu} is norm-equivalent to the Sobolev space Hs​(𝒳)H^{s}(\mathcal{X}) (Wendland 2005), equipped with the norm

‖f‖Hs​(𝒳)=(∑|α|≤s∫𝒳|∂αf⁡(x)|2​𝑑x)1/2,\|f\|_{H^{s}(\mathcal{X})}=\left(\sum_{|\alpha|\leq s}\int_{\mathcal{X}}|\partial^{\alpha}f(x)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\right)^{1/2},

where α=(α1,…,αdx)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d_{x}}) is a multi-index with |α|=α1+⋯+αdx|\alpha|=\alpha_{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{d_{x}}. On the compact domain 𝒳\mathcal{X}, any function that is ss times continuously differentiable belongs to Hs​(𝒳)H^{s}(\mathcal{X}). The regularity required by the RKHS approach can therefore be interpreted as requiring sufficient smoothness of h⁡(z,x)h(z,x) with respect to xx.

{assumption}

There exists B<∞B<\infty such that for every z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, h⁡(z,⋅)∈Hs​(𝒳)h(z;\cdot)\in H^{s}(\mathcal{X}) with ‖h⁡(z,⋅)‖Hs​(𝒳)≤B\|h(z;\cdot)\|_{H^{s}(\mathcal{X})}\leq B.

The smoothness index ss in Assumption 3.2 determines the extent to which KRR can exploit the regularity of h⁡(z,⋅)h(z;\cdot) to improve statistical efficiency. The following result quantifies this effect for the weighted empirical PtO objective constructed using KRR weights, and the proof is provided in Appendix 8.1.

Proposition 3.1

Suppose Assumptions 2–3.2 hold with s=ν+dx/2s=\nu+d_{x}/2 and ν>0\nu>0. Let h^n​(z,x)\hat{h}_{n}(z;x) be the weighted empirical PtO objective in Equation (4) constructed using the KRR weights ωN,iKRR​(x)\omega_{N,i}^{\mathrm{KRR}}(x) associated with the Matérn kernel KνK_{\nu}. Choosing the regularization parameter λn≍log⁡n/n\lambda_{n}\asymp\log n/n, we have

𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[h⁡(z^n​(X),X)−h⁡(z∗​(X),X)|𝒟n]]=𝒪⁡(n−ν2​ν+dx​(log⁡n)12).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbb{E}\!\left[h(\hat{z}_{n}(X);X)-h(z^{\ast}(X);X)\,\Big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\right]\right]\,=\,\mathcal{O}\!\left(n^{-\frac{\nu}{2\nu+d_{x}}}(\log n)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right).

The convergence rate n−ν/(2ν+dx)n^{-\nu/(2\nu+d_{x})} established in Proposition 3.1 formalizes the statistical efficiency of KRR. As the Sobolev smoothness of the conditional expectation h⁡(z,⋅)∈Hs​(𝒳)h(z;\cdot)\in H^{s}(\mathcal{X}) increases, i.e., as s=ν+dx/2s=\nu+d_{x}/2 grows, the exponent ν/(2​ν+dx)\nu/(2\nu+d_{x}) approaches 1/21/2, thereby progressively weakening the effect of the ambient dimension dxd_{x} on the convergence rate. In this sense, KRR-based PtO translates the smoothness of h⁡(z,⋅)h(z;\cdot) into improved statistical efficiency and mitigates the curse of dimensionality associated with local methods.

However, this gain in statistical efficiency comes at the cost of convexity preservation. Because KRR weights in Equation (4) are obtained through kernel matrix inversion, they are generally sign-indefinite. The presence of negative weights implies that h^n​(z,x)\hat{h}_{n}(z;x) is no longer a nonnegative combination of the per-sample cost c⁡(z,Xi,Yi)c(z;X_{i},Y_{i}). Consequently, even when each c⁡(z,⋅,⋅)c(z;\cdot,\cdot) is convex in zz, the resulting empirical PtO objective in Equation (4) need not remain convex, potentially complicating downstream optimization and increasing its computational burden (see Section 6.3.2 for an example).

Bertsimas and Koduri (2022) observe that the negative KRR weights are typically small in magnitude and propose clipping them at zero to restore convexity. Specifically, each negative weight is replaced by zero, thereby converting the estimated objective into a nonnegative combination of the per-sample cost functions. However, they do not establish theoretical guarantees for the statistical performance of the resulting clipped KRR estimator. In the next subsection, we show that although this clipped KRR method restores convexity, it also reintroduces the curse of dimensionality.

3.3 The Convexity–Efficiency Dilemma

The complementary strengths and limitations of local and global methods naturally raises a question: is it possible to design a prediction scheme for PtO that simultaneously preserve convexity and achieve statistical efficiency by overcoming the curse of dimensionality? Equivalently, can we construct a weighting scheme ωn,i\omega_{n,i} in Equation (3) that guarantees nonnegativity throughout the covariate space while exploiting high-order smoothness to achieve statistical efficiency in high-dimensional settings?

Our theoretical analysis in this subsection reveals that these two objectives are fundamentally mutually exclusive. To state the result formally, we adopt a minimax formulation over a class of smooth problem instances and a broad class of PtO procedures characterized only through their weighting rules.

{assumption}

[Problem Class for Minimax Lower Bound] Fix a nonnegative integer β\beta. Let 𝒫β\mathcal{P}_{\beta} denote a class of problem instances (P,c)(P,c), where PP is a joint distribution of (X,Y)(X,Y) supported on 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} and c:𝒵×𝒳×𝒴→ℝc:\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} is a measurable cost function. For each (P,c)∈𝒫β(P,c)\in\mathcal{P}_{\beta}, define the induced conditional objective h⁡(z,x):=𝔼P⁡[c⁡(z,X,Y)|X=x].h(z;x):=\E_{P}\!\left[c(z;X,Y)|X=x\right]. We assume the following conditions hold:

  • (i)

    For every fixed z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, the map x↦h⁡(z,x)x\mapsto h(z;x) is β\beta-times continuously differentiable on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, with all partial derivatives up to order β\beta uniformly bounded over 𝒳\mathcal{X}, where β=0\beta=0 means continuity.

  • (ii)

    The covariates are supported on the hypercube 𝒳=[0,1]dx\mathcal{X}=[0,1]^{d_{x}} and admit a density pp such that 0<pmin≤p⁡(x)≤pmax<∞0<p_{\min}\leq p(x)\leq p_{\max}<\infty for all x∈𝒳.x\in\mathcal{X}.

  • (iii)

    The conditional variance of YY given X=xX=x is uniformly lower bounded, i.e., 𝖵𝖺𝗋P⁡(Y|X=x)≥σ2\Var_{P}(Y|X=x)\geq\sigma^{2} for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and some constant σ>0\sigma>0.

{assumption}

[Admissible PtO Weights] A PtO algorithm is said to use admissible weights if, for every sample size nn, every query point x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, and every realization of x1:nx_{1:n}, it assigns weights {ωn,i​(x)}i=1n\{\omega_{n,i}(x)\}_{i=1}^{n} satisfying:

  • (i)

    Each ωn,i​(x)\omega_{n,i}(x) depends only on (x,x1:n)(x,x_{1:n}), and does not depend on y1:ny_{1:n}.

  • (ii)

    ωn,i​(x)≥0\omega_{n,i}(x)\geq 0 for all i=1,…,n.i=1,\dots,n.

  • (iii)

    ∑i=1nωn,i​(x)>0\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{n,i}(x)>0 for all x∈𝒳.x\in\mathcal{X}.

Theorem 3.2 (Minimax Lower Bound for Convexity-Preserving PtO)

Consider the setting dy=dz=1d_{y}=d_{z}=1 with 𝒴=𝒵=[−R,R]\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{Z}=[-R,R] for some sufficiently large R>0R>0. Fix a nonnegative integer β\beta, let 𝒫β\mathcal{P}_{\beta} be the problem class in Assumption 3.3. Consider any PtO algorithm that, given data 𝒟n={(xi,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{n}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} and a query covariate xx, constructs the empirical objective as Equation (3), where the weights satisfy Assumption 3.3, and outputs a decision z^n​(x)∈arg⁡minz∈𝒵​h^n​(z,x).\hat{z}_{n}(x)\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\hat{h}_{n}(z;x). Then there exists a constant c0>0c_{0}>0, independent of nn, such that

sup(P,c)∈𝒫β𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[h⁡(z^n​(X),X)−h⁡(z∗​(X),X)|𝒟n]]≥c0​n−4dx+4.\sup_{(P,c)\in\mathcal{P}_{\beta}}\E\left[\E\left[h(\hat{z}_{n}(X);X)-h(z^{\ast}(X);X)\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\right]\right]\ \geq\ c_{0}\,n^{-\frac{4}{d_{x}+4}}. (5)

Theorem 3.2 establishes a formal “no-free-lunch” result for PtO procedures using nonnegative, covariate-based weights satisfying Assumption 3.3. Even when the conditional objective is β\beta-times continuously differentiable for arbitrarily large β\beta, the worst-case expected regret of any such procedure cannot decay faster than n−4/(dx+4)n^{-4/(d_{x}+4)}. This limitation already arises with a one-dimensional outcome and decision, demonstrating that these weighting schemes can fail to fully exploit high-order smoothness even in this simple setting. This lower-bound rate coincides with that of second-order local methods and deteriorates rapidly as the covariate dimension dxd_{x} increases. Thus, nonnegativity constitutes a fundamental statistical bottleneck: although it preserves convexity, it prevents the estimator from attaining the faster convergence rates associated with global smoothers over highly smooth function classes.

The proof constructs a finite adversarial subclass of 𝒫β\mathcal{P}_{\beta}, consisting of instances whose conditional objectives are quadratic and strongly convex in the decision variable, such that, for any PtO algorithm whose weights satisfy Assumption 3.3, at least one instance in this subclass incurs expected regret at least of order n−4/(dx+4)n^{-4/(d_{x}+4)}. Taking the maximum over this finite subclass and subsequently the supremum over 𝒫β\mathcal{P}_{\beta} yields Equation (5). When ν=2\nu=2, the exponent in Proposition 3.1’s upper bound is half that in Theorem 3.2’s lower bound. This difference may be explained by the different proof arguments. Proposition 3.1 bounds regret by the uniform objective-estimation error without exploiting curvature, whereas Theorem 3.2 uses a quadratic construction in which regret is proportional to the squared decision error. Neither bound is guaranteed to be tight, and considering a more general adversarial subclass may yield a sharper lower bound. The complete proof of Theorem 3.2 is provided in Appendix 8.2.

To illustrate this dilemma, we consider a contextual newsvendor problem in which a retailer decides how much inventory to order each day. The resulting cost depends on both the order quantity zz and the realized demand YY. Specifically, the retailer incurs an overage cost when the order quantity exceeds demand and a shortage cost when demand exceeds the order quantity. At the time of ordering, the retailer does not observe demand YY, but has access to some covariates XX, such as seasonal conditions, promotional activities, and weather, that may help predict demand. The detailed experimental setting, including the cost parameters, conditional demand distribution is provided in Section 6.2. Here, we use the structure-aware formulation established in Section 6.2, under which the objective function is infinitely differentiable in xx. We fix the training sample size at n=2,000n=2,000 and vary the covariate dimension dxd_{x}. We evaluate decision performance using the relative cost defined in Equation (2), with unconditional SAA as the benchmark.

Figure 3.3 compares traditional local PtO methods with two variants of KRR-based PtO. PtO-KRR uses the original KRR weights, which can be negative, while PtO-KRR+ truncates negative weights to zero and renormalizes the remaining weights to sum to one, following Bertsimas and Koduri (2022). Traditional local methods, including kk-nearest neighbors and kernel smoothing, use nonnegative weights and therefore preserve convexity. Their performance, however, deteriorates substantially as dxd_{x} increases, illustrating the severe effect of the curse of dimensionality on local PtO methods. By contrast, PtO-KRR exploits the existing global smoothness and maintains relatively stable performance as dxd_{x} increases. PtO-KRR+ restores convexity through nonnegative weights but exhibits a similarly pronounced deterioration, indicating that clipping eliminates much of the high-dimensional advantage of the original KRR estimator. In summary, the theoretical and numerical results reveal a fundamental dilemma within standard PtO frameworks: preserving convexity through nonnegative weights and attaining high-dimensional statistical efficiency through high-order smoothness cannot, in general, be achieved simultaneously.

4 Generate-then-Optimize

We next introduce an alternative paradigm, Generate-then-Optimize (GtO), for solving the CSO problem (1). GtO is a standard simulation-based method for solving stochastic optimization problems, which can be naturally extended to the CSO problem (1). Denote FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) as the conditional distribution of YY conditioned on X=xX=x. On the offline stage, we use the historical data 𝒟n={(xi,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{n}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} to learn the conditional distribution or a simulator for Y|{X=x}Y|\{X=x\}, denoted as F^Y|X(⋅|x)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x). On the online stage, when a new covariate X=x0X=x_{0} arrives, we generate mm i.i.d. samples from F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}), denoted as Y^1,Y^2,…,Y^m∼F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{Y}_{1},\hat{Y}_{2},\ldots,\hat{Y}_{m}\sim\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}). Then, we can use SAA to construct a sample objective function h^\hat{h} and solve the simulation-based CSO problem accordingly as

z^n,m∗(x0)∈argminz∈𝒵{h^(z;x0):=1m∑j=1mc(z;x0,Y^j)}.\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0})\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\left\{\hat{h}(z;x_{0}):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}c\big(z;x_{0},\hat{Y}_{j}\big)\right\}. (6)

4.1 Convexity Preservation

Assumption 2 supposes that the cost function c⁡(z,x,y)c(z;x,y) is convex in zz for each fixed (x,y)(x,y). The following proposition shows that GtO preserve the convexity structure of the cost function.

Proposition 4.1

If c⁡(⋅,x,y)c(\cdot;x,y) is convex on 𝒵\mathcal{Z} for all (x,y)(x,y), then for any realized simulator F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}), the SAA objective h^​(z,x0):=1m​∑j=1mc⁡(z,x0,Y^j)\hat{h}(z;x_{0}):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}c(z;x_{0},\hat{Y}_{j}), where Y^1,Y^2,…,Y^m∼F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{Y}_{1},\hat{Y}_{2},\ldots,\hat{Y}_{m}\sim\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}), is convex on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}.

The proof of Proposition 4.1 is immediate from the fact that nonnegative linear combinations of convex functions are convex. Proposition 4.1 shows that, under GtO, the optimization problem (6) solved online is exactly a convex program with h^​(⋅,x0)\hat{h}(\cdot;x_{0}) being convex. Thus, the powerful machinery of convex optimization can be used without modification and classical stability results for convex stochastic programming apply; see, e.g., Shapiro et al. (2009).

4.2 Conditional Generative Models for GtO

The GtO framework is agnostic to the particular generative architecture used to construct F^Y|X(⋅|x)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x). Its essential requirement is a learned conditional distribution from which scenarios can be generated at a given covariate value. A conditional generator may be represented abstractly as Y^=Gθ^​(x,ξ)\hat{Y}=G_{\hat{\theta}}(x,\xi), where ξ∼Pξ\xi\sim P_{\xi}, Gθ^G_{\hat{\theta}} is learned from 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}, and the exogenous random variable ξ\xi supplies the randomness required for scenario generation. The distribution induced by Gθ^​(x,ξ)G_{\hat{\theta}}(x,\xi) defines F^Y|X(⋅|x)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x). This formulation encompasses both classical conditional distribution estimators that permit sampling and modern deep generative models. We focus on the latter.

A variety of conditional generative models can be incorporated into GtO. Representative examples include conditional variational autoencoders, which use latent variables to represent complex conditional distributions; conditional generative adversarial networks, which learn a conditional sampler through adversarial training; and conditional normalizing flows, which construct flexible conditional densities through invertible transformations. Autoregressive models can generate outcomes sequentially and are particularly useful for discrete, sequential, or otherwise structured outcomes. Transformer-based language models also belong to this class when outcomes are represented as sequences. We refer to Bond-Taylor et al. (2022) for a review of these model families. Conditional diffusion models provide another approach, generating scenarios through a learned reverse diffusion process (Yang et al. 2024). Related flow-matching models learn continuous transformations from a reference distribution to the target distribution through a vector-field regression objective.

We use conditional diffusion models (CDMs) as a benchmark implementation of GtO. They can flexibly represent high-dimensional and multimodal conditional distributions, and their denoising-based training avoids the adversarial minimax optimization used by conditional GANs. Recent studies also provide explicit statistical guarantees for conditional distribution estimation, making CDMs suitable for connecting our theoretical analysis with an implementable generative model (Fu et al. 2024, Tang et al. 2025). A potential limitation is the cost of generating samples through a discretized reverse-time process. Accelerated samplers and distillation methods can reduce this burden, although sampling cost remains an important consideration in downstream optimization; see Yang et al. (2024) for a review. Accordingly, we use CDMs in the subsequent theoretical and numerical analyses, while other conditional generative models can be incorporated into the same GtO framework.

We briefly describe the CDM. Fix a covariate value xx, and let {Yt:t≥0}\{Y_{t}:t\geq 0\} denote a forward Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process initialized from the target conditional distribution:

d​Yt=−12​Yt​d​t+d​Bt,with Y0∼FY|X(⋅|x) and t∈(0,T],\mathrm{d}Y_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}Y_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}B_{t},\quad\mbox{with $Y_{0}\sim F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x)$ and $t\in(0,T]$},

where BtB_{t} is a standard Brownian motion. Equivalently, Yt=atY0+btε,at=e−t/2,bt=1−e−t,ε∼𝒩(0,I).Y_{t}=a_{t}Y_{0}+b_{t}\varepsilon,~a_{t}=e^{-t/2},~b_{t}=\sqrt{1-e^{-t}},~\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). Let qt(⋅|x)q_{t}(\cdot|x) denote the conditional density of YtY_{t} given X=xX=x. The key object is the time-dependent conditional score s∗(y,x,t):=∇ylogqt(y|x),s^{\ast}(y,x,t):=\nabla_{y}\log q_{t}(y|x), which is estimated from 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} by denoising score matching. The conditional and unconditional score functions can be estimated jointly by minimizing the empirical denoising score-matching risk s^∈arg⁡mins∈𝒮​1n​∑i=1nℓ⁡(xi,yi,s),\hat{s}\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(x_{i},y_{i};s), where

ℓ(xi,yi;s):=1T−t0∫t0T𝔼τ,Y~t[‖s(Y~t,τ(xi),t)−∇y~logφt(Y~t∣yi)‖22]dt,\ell(x_{i},y_{i};s):=\frac{1}{T-t_{0}}\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tau,\tilde{Y}_{t}\end{subarray}}\left[\left\|s\big(\tilde{Y}_{t},\tau(x_{i}),t\big)-\nabla_{\tilde{y}}\log\varphi_{t}(\tilde{Y}_{t}\mid y_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]\mathrm{d}t,

where Y~t∼𝒩⁡(at​yi,bt2​I)\tilde{Y}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(a_{t}y_{i},b_{t}^{2}I), τ∼𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿​{∅,id}\tau\sim\mathsf{Unif}\{\varnothing,\mathrm{id}\}, τ⁡(xi)=xi\tau(x_{i})=x_{i} when τ=id\tau=\mathrm{id} and τ⁡(xi)=∅\tau(x_{i})=\varnothing when τ=∅\tau=\varnothing, and φt(⋅∣yi)\varphi_{t}(\cdot\mid y_{i}) denotes the Gaussian transition density 𝒩⁡(at​yi,bt2​I)\mathcal{N}(a_{t}y_{i},b_{t}^{2}I).
