(2024) and Fu et al. (2024) for more learning details. Given the estimated conditional score, scenarios are generated from the reverse-time stochastic differential equation

d​Y¯t=[12​Y¯t+s~​(Y¯t,x,T−t)]​d​t+d​B¯t,with Y¯0∼𝒩⁡(0,I) and t∈(0,T−t0],\mathrm{d}\bar{Y}_{t}=\left[\frac{1}{2}\bar{Y}_{t}+\tilde{s}\big(\bar{Y}_{t},x,T-t\big)\right]\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}\bar{B}_{t},\quad\mbox{with $\bar{Y}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and $t\in(0,T-t_{0}]$}, (7)

where B¯t\bar{B}_{t} is another Brownian motion independent of BtB_{t} and s~​(y,x,t):=(1+η)​s^​(y,x,t)−η​s^​(y,∅,t)\tilde{s}(y,x,t):=(1+\eta)\hat{s}(y,x,t)-\eta\hat{s}(y,\varnothing,t) with a guidance strength η≥0\eta\geq 0. For the distribution-estimation interpretation and the theoretical guarantees below, we take η=0\eta=0; positive values of η\eta correspond to an optional classifier-free guidance heuristic. At the population level, with the exact conditional score s∗s^{\ast}, the output distribution of the reverse-time process (7) approaches FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) as the terminal time TT becomes large and the early-stopping time t0t_{0} becomes small. In practice, using a finite TT and a positive t0t_{0}, replacing the exact score s∗s^{\ast} with an estimated score s~\tilde{s}, and numerically discretizing the reverse process yield the learned conditional distribution F^Y|X(⋅|x)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) from which GtO scenarios are generated. Under suitable assumptions and parameter choices, Fu et al. (2024) and Tang et al. (2025) establish convergence guarantees for such CDM estimators.

The regret analysis developed below deliberately abstracts away from these architectural details. It requires only that the learned model support conditionally independent scenario generation and that the discrepancy between F^Y|X(⋅|x)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) and FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) admit an appropriate statistical bound. The specific generative architecture affects the resulting regret bound only through the offline model error, while the online SAA error is governed by the number mm of generated scenarios. CDMs provide one concrete implementation for which theoretical distributional learning rates are available, but the GtO framework and the regret decomposition are not restricted to this particular model class.

4.3 Statistical Efficiency of GtO

Now, we analyze the regret

ℛ⁡(x0):=h⁡(z^n,m∗​(x0),x0)−h⁡(z∗​(x0),x0)≥0.\mathcal{R}(x_{0}):=h\left(\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0}\right)-h\left(z^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0}\right)\geq 0.

To isolate the impact of the model error from the SAA error, we define an auxiliary decision rule as

z¯n∗(x0)∈argminz∈𝒵{h¯(z;x0):=𝔼[c(z;X,Y^)|X=x0]},\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0})\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\Big\{\bar{h}(z;x_{0}):=\E\big[c(z;X,\hat{Y})\,|\,X=x_{0}\big]\Big\}, (8)

where Y^∼F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{Y}\sim\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}). Then we have the basic decomposition

ℛ⁡(x0)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(x_{0})
=[h⁡(z^n,m∗​(x0),x0)−h¯​(z^n,m∗​(x0),x0)]+[h¯​(z^n,m∗​(x0),x0)−h¯​(z¯n∗​(x0),x0)]+[h¯​(z¯n∗​(x0),x0)−h⁡(z∗​(x0),x0)]\displaystyle\,=\,\left[h(\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})-\bar{h}(\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})\right]+\left[\bar{h}(\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})-\bar{h}(\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})\right]+\left[\bar{h}(\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})-h(z^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})\right]
≤[h¯​(z^n,m∗​(x0),x0)−h¯​(z¯n∗​(x0),x0)]+2​supz∈𝒵|h⁡(z,x0)−h¯​(z,x0)|.\displaystyle\,\leq\,\left[\bar{h}(\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})-\bar{h}(\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})\right]+2\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\big|h(z;x_{0})-\bar{h}(z;x_{0})\big|. (9)

The first term in Equation (9) is the error induced by the SAA under the distribution F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}), while the second term in Equation (9) is the model error caused by the difference between F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}) and FY|X(⋅|x0)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}). We will discuss the two terms in Equation (9) separately, and then summarize their combined impact on the regret ℛ⁡(x0)\mathcal{R}(x_{0}).

4.3.1 The SAA Error.

We first analyze the contribution of the SAA approximation to the regret in Equation (9). Fix the covariate value x0x_{0}, and treat the offline data 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} and the learned distribution or simulator F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}) as given. All expectations in this subsection are taken with respect to the simulation draws Y^1,Y^2,…,Y^m\hat{Y}_{1},\hat{Y}_{2},\dots,\hat{Y}_{m} conditional on 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} and X=x0X=x_{0}.

Lemma 4.2

Suppose Assumption 2 holds. Fix a covariate value x0x_{0} and a realization of the learned conditional distribution or simulator F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}). Then there exists a constant CSAA<∞C_{\mathrm{SAA}}<\infty, depending only on (G,M,D,dz)(G,M,D,d_{z}), such that for all m≥2m\geq 2,

𝔼[h¯(z^n,m∗(x0);x0)−h¯(z¯n∗(x0);x0)|𝒟n,X=x0]≤CSAAm−1/2.\E\left[\bar{h}(\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})-\bar{h}(\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n},X=x_{0}\right]\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{SAA}}\,m^{-1/2}. (10)

Lemma 4.2 shows that, once the learned distribution or simulator F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}) is fixed, the SAA-based decision z^n,m∗\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast} is nearly optimal for the population objective z¯n∗​(x0)\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0}), with regret decaying at the typical rate m−1/2m^{-1/2} which comes from the fact that h^\hat{h} is an empirical average of mm i.i.d. samples. The proof follows the standard SAA/M-estimation pattern: obtain a uniform bound on the empirical objective and then transfer it to the regret; see, e.g., van der Vaart (1998, Chapter 5) and Shapiro et al. (2009, Chapter 5). The existing SAA results typically provide almost-sure or in-probability convergence of regrets and solutions, and asymptotic distributions; see, e.g., Shapiro et al. (2009), Banholzer et al. (2022). Our result here is a non-asymptotic L1L^{1}-error bound for the SAA regret with explicit m−1/2m^{-1/2} dependence. We provide the proof in Appendix 9.1.

4.3.2 The Model Error.

We now turn to the contribution of model misspecification, i.e., the error caused by using the learned conditional distribution F^Y|X\hat{F}_{Y|X} instead of the true distribution FY|XF_{Y|X}.

{assumption}

There exist constants CM>0C_{\mathrm{M}}>0, α0>0\alpha_{0}>0, and α1≥0\alpha_{1}\geq 0 such that for all n≥2n\geq 2,

𝔼[𝔼[TV(F^Y|X(⋅|X),FY|X(⋅|X))|𝒟n]]≤CMn−α0(logn)α1,\E\Big[\E\Big[\mathrm{TV}\Big(\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|X),F_{Y|X}(\cdot|X)\Big)\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\Big]\Big]\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{M}}\,n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}, (11)

where TV\mathrm{TV} denotes the total variation distance, the inner expectation is with respect to the covariate XX, and the outer expectation is with respect to the training data 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}.

Assumption 4.3.2 requires that the learned conditional distribution F^Y|X(⋅|x)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) converges to the true conditional distribution FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) in total variation, on average over the covariate distribution, at some explicit rate n−α0n^{-\alpha_{0}} up to logarithmic factors. Such rates are available in both parametric and nonparametric settings. In parametric conditional density models with a finite-dimensional parameter estimated at the usual n−1/2n^{-1/2} rate (van der Vaart 1998), one can show that Assumption 4.3.2 holds with α0=1/2\alpha_{0}=1/2 and α1=0\alpha_{1}=0 under some regularity conditions. In nonparametric conditional density estimation, minimax rates in integrated L1L_{1} (and hence total variation) risk of the form n−β/(dx+dy+2β)n^{-\beta/(d_{x}+d_{y}+2\beta)} with log factors are attainable under β\beta-Hölder smoothness assumptions; see, e.g., Tsybakov (2009), Li et al. (2022), Fu et al. (2024).

Remark 4.3

Recently, Fu et al. (2024) study the sample complexity of using CDMs to estimate the conditional distribution FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) from data. Under their baseline conditions, the conditional density pY|X​(y|x)p_{Y|X}(y|x) satisfies a uniform Gaussian-type upper-tail bound and β\beta-Hölder smooth (i.e., belongs to a β\beta-Hölder ball). Together with a uniform bound on its Kullback–Leibler divergence from the standard Gaussian distribution and appropriate choices of the early-stopping and terminal times, their result yields

α0=β4​(dx+dy+β)andα1=max⁡{9,dy2+β4+1}.\alpha_{0}=\frac{\beta}{4(d_{x}+d_{y}+\beta)}\quad\text{and}\quad\alpha_{1}=\max\left\{9,\,\frac{d_{y}}{2}+\frac{\beta}{4}+1\right\}.

Furthermore, under their stronger conditional-density condition, pY|X(y|x)=exp(−C2∥y∥22/2)⋅f(y,x),p_{Y|X}(y|x)=\textrm{exp}(-C_{2}\|y\|_{2}^{2}/2)\cdot f(y,x), where ff is β\beta-Hölder smooth and is uniformly bounded away from zero, the rate improves to

α0=βdx+dy+2​βandα1=max⁡{192,β+22}.\alpha_{0}=\frac{\beta}{d_{x}+d_{y}+2\beta}\quad\text{and}\quad\alpha_{1}=\max\left\{\frac{19}{2},\,\frac{\beta+2}{2}\right\}.

Consequently, for fixed dxd_{x} and dyd_{y}, the convergence rate α0\alpha_{0} approach 1/21/2 as β→∞\beta\to\infty. Similarly, Tang et al. (2025) establish a related rate under compact-support and smooth conditional-density assumptions, while allowing the smoothness levels in the covariate and response directions to differ. Assumption 4.3.2 therefore summarizes the statistical accuracy of the offline conditional-distribution learning step in a form directly applicable to our regret analysis.

Lemma 4.4

Suppose Assumptions 2 and 4.3.2 hold. Then

𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[supz∈𝒵|h⁡(z,X)−h¯​(z,X)||𝒟n]]≤ 2​M​CM​n−α0​(log⁡n)α1,\E\Big[\E\Big[\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}|h(z;X)-\bar{h}(z;X)|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\Big]\Big]\;\leq\;2M\,C_{\mathrm{M}}\,n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}, (12)

where the inner expectation is with respect to XX and the outer expectation is with respect to 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}.

Lemma 4.4 shows that, under the average total variation convergence of Assumption 4.3.2, the regret due purely to model misspecification (i.e., optimizing under F^Y|X(⋅|x)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) instead of FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x)) decays at the same rate as the simulator itself in total variation, up to constants depending on the cost envelope MM. We arrange the proof in Appendix 9.2.

Remark 4.5 (Alternative Distributional Discrepancies)

Assumption 4.3.2 is stated in terms of total variation because, under the uniform boundedness condition |c⁡(z,x,y)|≤M|c(z;x,y)|\leq M, total variation directly controls the discrepancy between the true and learned conditional objectives as shown in Appendix 9.2. More generally, the same analysis applies to a probability metric or statistical divergence ρ\rho whenever there exist constants Lρ<∞L_{\rho}<\infty and γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1] such that

supz∈𝒵|𝔼Y∼P⁡[c⁡(z,x,Y)]−𝔼Y∼Q⁡[c⁡(z,x,Y)]|≤Lρ​ρ​(P,Q)γ\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\left|\E_{Y\sim P}[c(z;x,Y)]-\E_{Y\sim Q}[c(z;x,Y)]\right|\,\leq\,L_{\rho}\rho(P,Q)^{\gamma} (13)

for all relevant distributions PP and QQ. Furthermore, if

𝔼[𝔼[ρ(F^Y|X(⋅|X),FY|X(⋅|X))|𝒟n]]≤CMn−α0(logn)α1,\E\Big[\E\Big[\rho\Big(\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|X),F_{Y|X}(\cdot|X)\Big)\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\Big]\Big]\,\leq\,C_{\mathrm{M}}n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}, (14)

then the proof of Lemma 4.4 and Jensen’s inequality yield

𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[supz∈𝒵|h⁡(z,X)−h¯​(z,X)||𝒟n]]≤Lρ​CMγ​n−γ​α0​(log⁡n)γ​α1.\E\Big[\E\Big[\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}|h(z;X)-\bar{h}(z;X)|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\Big]\Big]\,\leq\,L_{\rho}C_{\mathrm{M}}^{\gamma}n^{-\gamma\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\gamma\alpha_{1}}.

For bounded costs, Condition (13) holds with (Lρ,γ)=(2​M,1)(L_{\rho},\gamma)=(2M,1) for total variation, (2​2​M,1)(2\sqrt{2}M,1) for the Hellinger distance, and (2​M,1/2)(\sqrt{2}M,1/2) for the Kullback–Leibler divergence. If c(z;x,⋅)c(z;x,\cdot) is uniformly LyL_{y}-Lipschitz, it also holds with (Lρ,γ)=(Ly,1)(L_{\rho},\gamma)=(L_{y},1) for the pp-Wasserstein distance with p≥1p\geq 1.

Distributional learning rates (14) under these discrepancies are available for several of the conditional generative models discussed in Section 4.2. In particular, explicit total-variation and Wasserstein rates have been established for CDMs (Fu et al. 2024, Tang et al. 2025). For adversarial generators, Liu et al. (2021) establish nonasymptotic distributional guarantees for a Wasserstein-based conditional generator, which can be viewed as a conditional WGAN-type approach. For latent-variable models, Kumar et al. (2025) derive Hellinger and Wasserstein convergence rates for a likelihood-based conditional deep generative model and implement the estimator using a conditional VAE architecture. Closely related to flow-matching models, Huang et al. (2023) establish nonasymptotic guarantees for conditional stochastic interpolation, which constructs conditional samplers through learned probability-flow ODEs or stochastic differential equations. Comparable distributional learning rates are, to our knowledge, less developed for general conditional normalizing flows and Transformer-based autoregressive generators. Importantly, these guarantees apply to the specific estimators and regularity conditions studied in the respective works, rather than uniformly to the corresponding generative-model architecture classes.

4.3.3 Regret Bound for GtO.

We now combine the SAA regret bound (Lemma 4.2) and the model regret bound (Lemma 4.4) to obtain an overall bound on the regret of the GtO procedure. Taking expectations over the randomness in both the training data and the online covariate on both sides of Equation (9), and applying Lemmas 4.2 and 4.4, yields the desired regret bound.

Theorem 4.6

Suppose Assumptions 2 and 4.3.2 hold. Then there exists a constant C<∞C<\infty, depending only on (G,M,D,dz,CM,α0,α1)(G,M,D,d_{z},C_{\mathrm{M}},\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1}), such that for all integers n,m≥2n,m\geq 2,

𝔼[𝔼[h(z^n,m∗(X);X)−h(z∗(X);X)|𝒟n]]≤C(n−α0(logn)α1+m−1/2),\E\Big[\E\Big[h(\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(X);X)-h(z^{\ast}(X);X)\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\Big]\Big]\;\leq\;C\left(n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}+m^{-1/2}\right), (15)

where, conditional on 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}, the inner expectation is with respect to the online covariate XX and the conditional simulation draws, and the outer expectation is with respect to 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}.

Theorem 4.6 provides a clean decomposition of the average regret of the GtO procedure into: an offline learning error term, n−α0​(log⁡n)α1n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}, which reflects how accurately the conditional distribution FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) can be learned from nn samples in total variation, and an online SAA error term, m−1/2m^{-1/2}, which reflects the Monte Carlo error from using mm simulated samples at decision time. In the situation where α0=1/2\alpha_{0}=1/2 (Remark 4.3), this yields the canonical rate

𝔼[𝔼[h(z^n,m∗(X);X)−h(z∗(X);X)|𝒟n]]=𝒪(n−1/2(logn)α1+m−1/2)=𝒪~(n−1/2+m−1/2).\E\Big[\E\Big[h(\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(X);X)-h(z^{\ast}(X);X)\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\Big]\Big]\,=\,\mathcal{O}\Big(n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}+m^{-1/2}\Big)\,=\,\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\Big(n^{-1/2}+m^{-1/2}\Big).

Theorem 4.6 makes explicit the trade-off between investing in more training data (larger nn) and using more simulation at decision time (larger mm). In particular, if one balances the two error terms by choosing mm as a suitable function of nn, the overall regret can be minimized. We arrange the proof in Appendix 9.3.

Remark 4.7

Furthermore, if the cost function c⁡(z,x,y)c(z;x,y) is strongly convex on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, then we can improve the result (15) to

𝔼[𝔼[∥z^n,m∗(X)−z∗(X)∥|𝒟n]]≤C(n−α0(logn)α1+m−1/2),\E\Big[\E\Big[\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(X)-z^{\ast}(X)\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\Big]\Big]\;\leq\;C\left(n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}+m^{-1/2}\right), (16)

for some constant CC depending on the setting of strongly convex cost function; See Appendix 9.4 for the detailed discussion.

5 Choosing Between Predictive and Generative Approaches

Our analysis yields three managerial insights for choosing between PtO and GtO, concerning the statistical difficulty of the learning target, the optimization structure retained after learning, and the range of decisions the learned model will support. These insights explain why neither approach is uniformly preferable and provide practical guidance on where an organization can invest to improve its decision process.

5.1 Learning Less Is Not Always Easier

PtO learns the conditional expected objective h⁡(z,x)h(z;x), whereas GtO learns the conditional uncertainty underlying that objective. Although the former is a narrower target, its statistical difficulty depends on its smoothness. To illustrate this distinction, consider the specific guarantees established earlier for KRR-based PtO and CDM-based GtO. Under suitable regularity conditions, suppressing logarithmic factors and the finite-scenario approximation error gives

𝔼⁡[ℛPtO]≲n−αP\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{PtO}}\right]\lesssim n^{-\alpha_{P}}\quad where αP=βh/(2​βh+dx),\displaystyle\quad\alpha_{P}=\beta_{h}/(2\beta_{h}+d_{x}),
𝔼⁡[ℛGtO]≲n−αG\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{GtO}}\right]\lesssim n^{-\alpha_{G}}\quad where αG=βF/(2​βF+dx+dy).\displaystyle\quad\alpha_{G}=\beta_{F}/(2\beta_{F}+d_{x}+d_{y}).

Here, βh=sh−dx/2>0\beta_{h}=s_{h}-d_{x}/2>0 represents the expected-objective smoothness parameter in the KRR bound, and βF\beta_{F} is the conditional-density smoothness parameter in the CDM bound.

These expressions reveal a tradeoff between dimension and smoothness. GtO bears the additional dimension dyd_{y}, but its learning target can be smoother than the expected objective. PtO avoids that additional dimension, while its convergence rate also depends on the regularity of the expected objective. Thus, identifying the smaller learning target is not enough; one must also identify which target is easier to learn.

5.2 Statistical Flexibility Has an Optimization Consequence

Convexity is an important source of tractability in optimization, but whether it survives learning depends on how the estimated objective is constructed. Both PtO and GtO use weighted combinations of scenario costs:

h^P​(z,x)=∑i=1nωn,i​(x)​c​(z,Xi,Yi),h^G​(z,x)=1m​∑j=1mc⁡(z,x0,Y~j).\hat{h}_{P}(z;x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{n,i}(x)\,c(z;X_{i},Y_{i}),\qquad\hat{h}_{G}(z;x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}c(z;x_{0},\tilde{Y}_{j}).

When c⁡(⋅,x,y)c(\cdot;x,y) is convex for every (x,y)(x,y), nonnegative weights preserve convexity. GtO uses equal positive weights and therefore inherits this property. PtO, however, faces the dilemma established by our earlier lower-bound result: within the class of nonnegative, covariate-based weighting rules studied there, worst-case expected regret cannot decay faster than n−4/(dx+4)n^{-4/(d_{x}+4)}, even for arbitrarily smooth objectives in the constructed problem class. Thus, nonnegative weighting preserves convexity but limits the statistical gains available from additional smoothness. More flexible regression can exploit that smoothness, but may introduce negative weights and lose the general convexity guarantee.

Negative weights do not necessarily make the fitted objective nonconvex, nor does nonconvexity necessarily make it difficult to optimize. Their computational effect depends on the problem’s structure. The numerical study illustrates this distinction: the signed weighted newsvendor objective in Section 6.2 remains efficiently solvable, whereas signed weights can invalidate the usual linear programming reformulation of the product placement problem in Section 6.3. Thus, the relevant concern is whether the fitted objective retains the structure needed by the solution method.

Convexity alone also does not determine computational cost. For GtO, the bound 𝔼[ℛGtO]≲δn+m−1/2\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{GtO}}]\lesssim\delta_{n}+m^{-1/2} highlights the role of scenario count: increasing mm reduces scenario approximation error but increases the scenario generation cost and enlarges the optimization problem, without eliminating model error δn\delta_{n}. PtO’s computational cost likewise depends on its fitted representation and the available solver. The two approaches should therefore be compared by the decision quality they deliver within the available computational budget.

5.3 The Appropriate Learning Target Depends on the Scope of Reuse

The preceding discussion focuses on a single decision problem. An organization may instead face a collection of tasks that share the same conditional uncertainty:

minz∈𝒵k⁡hk​(z,x),hk​(z,x)=𝔼⁡[ck​(z,X,Y)∣X=x],k=1,…,K.\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{k}}h_{k}(z;x),\qquad h_{k}(z;x)=\mathbb{E}[c_{k}(z;X,Y)\mid X=x],\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.

The costs and constraints may differ across tasks, even though the relevant uncertain outcomes are the same.

This distinction changes the value of what is learned. A model tailored to hkh_{k} can focus its statistical capacity on one task. A conditional generator can support multiple tasks through h^G,k​(z,x)=m−1​∑j=1mck​(z,x,Y~j)\hat{h}_{G,k}(z;x)=m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_{k}(z;x,\tilde{Y}_{j}). Once generated, the same scenarios can be evaluated under different objectives and constraints. Learning a richer object can therefore have value beyond its performance on any single task.

This potential benefit is particularly relevant when data analysis and operations reside in different departments. A shared generator provides an interface through which the data team supplies conditional scenarios and operational teams formulate their own decision problems. Changes in an objective need not require redesigning the learning target, provided the modeled uncertainty remains appropriate. This can reduce the coordination required to adapt analytics to new uses.

Reuse is nevertheless not exclusive to GtO. PtO methods can share weights, features, or estimated components across tasks. Nor does a generator remain valid automatically when a new task changes the underlying uncertainty — for example, when a pricing decision changes demand. The practical question is how much additional learning, validation, and coordination each new use requires.

Accordingly, the comparison should reflect the intended scope of deployment. For a stable, specialized task, exploiting objective-specific structure may be especially valuable. For a collection of evolving tasks with common uncertainty, a reusable generative model may justify its greater statistical and computational demands. The single-task regret bounds clarify those demands; they do not quantify the organizational benefits of reuse.

5.4 Practical Rules of Thumb

Taken together, these insights suggest choosing between PtO and GtO by considering what must be learned, how the resulting decision problem will be solved, and how broadly the model will be used. PtO’s specialization is valuable when it reduces the learning burden while retaining a tractable decision problem. GtO’s broader representation is valuable when regularity in the uncertainty, preservation of optimization structure, or reuse across tasks compensates for its additional learning and computational demands. Table 1 summarizes these considerations as practical rules of thumb. When the factors point in different directions, the final choice should be guided by decision quality and computational cost in the intended application.

6 Numerical Study

We compare PtO and GtO in three settings. A contextual newsvendor experiment examines the roles of training sample size, covariate dimension, and the structure of the learning target. A product placement experiment examines the computational consequences of signed prediction weights and the effect of outcome dimension. A fresh-retail inventory study evaluates the methods with real data at different levels of pooling. Together, the experiments compare decision quality and the computation required to obtain those decisions.

6.1 General Setup

The PtO benchmarks are kk-nearest neighbors (KNN), kernel smoothing (KS), kernel ridge regression (KRR), and clipped KRR (KRR+), which replaces negative weights by zero and renormalizes the remaining weights. For n≥10,000n\geq 10{,}000, KRR and clipped KRR use a Nyström approximation (Williams and Seeger 2001); the table headings retain the KRR designation. In the synthetic experiments, GtO uses a conditional diffusion model (GtO-CDM) (Fu et al. 2024). Unconditional SAA and an oracle based on the true data-generating process provide benchmarks. Hyperparameters are selected by validation decision cost and fixed before test evaluation.

Synthetic decision performance is measured by the relative cost in Section 2: RC=(CSAA−C)/(CSAA−Coracle)\mathrm{RC}=(C_{\mathrm{SAA}}-C)/(C_{\mathrm{SAA}}-C_{\mathrm{oracle}}). A larger value is better, with zero corresponding to SAA and one to the oracle. The retail study instead reports cost relative to SAA because the true conditional demand distribution is unavailable. Online time excludes model training and includes query-specific computations: prediction weights and optimization for PtO, and conditional scenario generation and optimization for GtO.

All experiments are implemented in Python 3.12.4 and run on the University of Minnesota Supercomputing Institute cluster with NVIDIA A40 GPUs and on Nanjing University servers with NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Gurobi 13.0.1 solves the product placement linear programs (LPs) and the convex subproblems in the difference-of-convex algorithm (DCA). Online time starts when a new context is observed and excludes model training. It includes computing prediction weights and solving the decision problem for PtO, and generating conditional scenarios and solving the decision problem for GtO.

6.2 Contextual Newsvendor Problem

We begin with a contextual newsvendor problem, in which a retailer uses observed covariates to determine an order quantity before demand is realized. A distinctive feature of our setting is a shortage penalty that changes discontinuously with the covariates, even though the conditional demand model varies smoothly. This allows us to examine how the comparison between PtO and GtO depends on whether PtO directly learns the objective or exploits its known structure. Details of the demand and cost construction are provided in Appendix 10.1.

6.2.1 Experimental Design.

After observing covariates X=x0X=x_{0}, the decision maker chooses an order quantity to solve

minz≥0⁡𝔼⁡[ch​(z−Y)++b⁡(X)​(Y−z)+∣X=x0],\min_{z\geq 0}\;\mathbb{E}\left[c_{h}(z-Y)^{+}+b(X)(Y-z)^{+}\mid X=x_{0}\right], (17)

where ch=90c_{h}=90. Conditional demand follows a three-component Gaussian mixture censored at zero. Covariates affect the component means, probabilities, and variances; average demand and signal-to-noise ratios are calibrated to remain comparable across dimensions. The known shortage penalty b⁡(x)b(x) takes 11 levels between 30 and 120 and is a step function of a covariate-based priority score.

We vary n∈{800,2000,5000,10000,20000,30000}n\in\{800,2000,5000,10000,20000,30000\} and dx∈{3,6,10,20,40,60,100}d_{x}\in\{3,6,10,20,40,60,100\}, holding dy=1d_{y}=1. Each setting uses 100 test contexts and 30 independent replications. To distinguish direct objective fitting from exploitation of known structure, we implement PtO in two ways:

h^ndirect​(z,x0)\displaystyle\hat{h}_{n}^{\mathrm{direct}}(z;x_{0}) =∑i=1nωn,i​(x0)​[ch​(z−yi)++b⁡(xi)​(yi−z)+],\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{n,i}(x_{0})\left[c_{h}(z-y_{i})^{+}+b(x_{i})(y_{i}-z)^{+}\right],
h^nstruct​(z,x0)\displaystyle\hat{h}_{n}^{\mathrm{struct}}(z;x_{0}) =∑i=1nωn,i​(x0)​[ch​(z−yi)++b⁡(x0)​(yi−z)+].\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{n,i}(x_{0})\left[c_{h}(z-y_{i})^{+}+b(x_{0})(y_{i}-z)^{+}\right].

The direct formulation estimates the conditional expected objective from historical costs, including the discontinuities in b⁡(x)b(x). The structure-aware formulation estimates expected overage and shortage separately and applies the known penalty at the current context. The two learning targets of this formulation, 𝔼⁡[(z−Y)+|X=x]\E[(z-Y)^{+}|X=x] and 𝔼⁡[(Y−z)+|X=x]\E[(Y-z)^{+}|X=x], are both smooth in xx under the demand model, whereas the overall objective learned by the direct formulation is discontinuous. This comparison therefore examines the value of learning a smoother objective in PtO by exploiting known cost structure while holding the underlying decision problem fixed.

6.2.2 Decision Quality and Computation.

Figure 6.2.2 compares GtO with the best-performing PtO benchmark in each setting. Each cell reports the difference in relative cost, GtO minus the best PtO; positive values favor GtO. The best PtO score summarizes the benchmark results rather than specifying an additional method for deployment. Tables 10.1.2 and 10.1.2 in Appendix 10.1.2 report the individual methods’ scores for the direct and structure-aware formulations, respectively. The GtO scores are identical across the two formulations.

Three patterns emerge. First, PtO is competitive with limited training data, while GtO’s relative performance improves as nn increases. At n=800n=800, the best PtO benchmark outperforms GtO in three of the seven covariate dimensions under each formulation; at n=2000n=2000, it does so in four of seven. At n=20,000n=20{,}000, GtO performs better in all seven dimensions under direct learning and six of seven under structure-aware learning. At n=30,000n=30{,}000, GtO performs better throughout. Thus, the larger-sample results favor GtO, although the ranking at smaller sample sizes depends on the context dimension and formulation.

Second, increasing the covariate dimension generally reduces decision performance, with a larger decline for PtO in several settings. At n=30,000n=30{,}000, increasing dxd_{x} from 3 to 100 reduces the best direct PtO score from 0.9899 to 0.6564 and the best structure-aware PtO score from 0.9804 to 0.7060, compared with a decline from 0.9943 to 0.8665 for GtO. The pattern is not monotonic in every setting, but these results illustrate the difficulty of high-dimensional objective fitting even when known cost structure is incorporated. They do not imply that high covariate dimension intrinsically favors GtO.

Third, incorporating objective structure changes the comparison, but does not uniformly improve finite-sample performance. At n=5000n=5000 and dx=20d_{x}=20, KRR’s relative cost increases from 0.7670 under direct learning to 0.8404 under structure-aware learning, reversing its ranking against GtO’s 0.7723. A similar reversal occurs at dx=40d_{x}=40, where KRR increases from 0.6402 to 0.8048, compared with GtO’s 0.7935. Across all seven dimensions at this sample size, PtO leads in two settings under direct learning and four under structure-aware learning. However, at n=30,000n=30{,}000 and dx=10d_{x}=10, KRR’s score falls from 0.8993 to 0.8062. Exploiting the smoothness of the learning targets therefore provides an opportunity to improve PtO, rather than a guarantee of better decisions in every setting.

The gains in decision quality can require substantially more online computation. Table 6.2.2 reports the structure-aware results at n=10,000n=10{,}000: PtO takes approximately 0.013 to 0.042 seconds per decision, whereas GtO takes 0.76 to 2.80 seconds. The empirical objectives are one-dimensional and piecewise linear, allowing breakpoint-based optimization even with signed weights when the objective is bounded below. Conditional scenario generation adds computation for GtO. The complete timing grids in Tables 10.1.2 and 10.1.2 show that this latency difference persists under both formulations. Thus, the more favorable GtO decision performance in many settings comes with a higher online computational cost.

6.3 Product Placement Problem

We next consider a product placement problem, in which a retailer allocates inventory across stores before demand is realized and subsequently transfers stock among stores to meet demand (Bertsimas and Koduri 2022). This setting introduces multivariate uncertainty, with the initial inventory decision having the same dimension as the demand vector. More importantly, this setting allows us to examine the computational consequences of signed PtO weights as the decision dimension increases. In the newsvendor problem, the decision is one-dimensional, so even when KRR produces negative weights, the piecewise-linear objective can be globally minimized by evaluating its breakpoints. In contrast, the product placement problem also has a piecewise-linear objective, but with a higher decision dimension, the number of candidate vertices can grow rapidly. Enumerating these candidates therefore becomes computationally impractical as dzd_{z} increases. We therefore need to exploit the structure of the optimization problem to using specific optimization algorithm to solve it.

The product placement problem has a two-stage linear structure. With nonnegative scenario weights, the second-stage optimization problems can be incorporated into the first-stage optimization, yielding a single linear program (LP) that can be efficiently solved even in higher dimensions. However, signed KRR weights invalidate this reformulation and may result in a nonconvex optimization problem. We therefore use a difference-of-convex algorithm (DCA) with linear programming subproblems; the derivation is provided in Appendix 10.2.2. Since DCA does not generally guarantee global optimality, the reported KRR results may also be affected by optimization error. Unlike the one-dimensional newsvendor problem, the computational cost of handling signed weights can become substantial as the decision dimension dzd_{z} increases. Details of the network, demand model, and optimization formulations are provided in Appendix 10.2.

6.3.1 Experimental Design.

Let zz denote initial inventory at the dyd_{y} stores and yy the realized demand vector. The recourse cost is

Q(z,y)=minf,p{g⊤f+r⊤p:z−Af+p≥y,f≥0,p≥0},Q(z,y)=\min_{f,p}\left\{g^{\top}f+r^{\top}p:\ z-Af+p\geq y,\ f\geq 0,\ p\geq 0\right\},

where ff denotes transfers, pp unmet demand, AA the network incidence matrix, and gg and rr the transportation and shortage cost vectors. The retailer minimizes α⊤​z+𝔼⁡[Q⁡(z,Y)∣X=x0]\alpha^{\top}z+\mathbb{E}[Q(z,Y)\mid X=x_{0}] over 0≤z≤U0\leq z\leq U, where α\alpha denotes placement costs and UU inventory upper bounds. Placement, transportation, and shortage costs are 2, 1, and 10 per unit, respectively. We extend the newsvendor demand model to correlated multivariate demand, fix n=10,000n=10{,}000 and dx=10d_{x}=10, and vary dy∈{1,2,5,10,15}d_{y}\in\{1,2,5,10,15\}.

6.3.2 Decision Quality and Solution Time.

Table 6.3.2 reports decision performance and online time together. We first compare the PtO methods. KRR consistently improves on clipped KRR: its relative cost lies between approximately 0.65 and 0.70, compared with 0.42–0.65 for clipped KRR. The improvement comes with longer solution times in every setting. At dy=15d_{y}=15, KRR achieves a relative cost of 0.6602 in 272.54 seconds, whereas clipped KRR achieves 0.4227 in 22.50 seconds. KNN and KS are faster still, but provide lower decision quality than raw KRR. These comparisons among PtO methods expose a clear tradeoff between decision quality and solution time.

Now we compare GtO with PtO algorithms in Table 6.3.2, in particular, we look at GtO-CDM. It achieves the highest relative cost in every tested setting, approximately 0.91–0.93, but is not uniformly the fastest approach. Its online times are comparable to raw PtO-KRR in several settings, and their ordering changes with dimension. At dy=1d_{y}=1, PtO-KRR takes 1.23 seconds compared with 2.95 seconds for GtO-CDM; at dy=15d_{y}=15, GtO-CDM takes 180.93 seconds compared with PtO-KRR’s 272.54 seconds. Nonnegative-weight PtO remains faster than either at the latter dimension. Even with the increased computational cost associated with signed weights, PtO-KRR achieves substantially lower decision quality than GtO-CDM despite their comparable online times in several settings. This comparison further highlights the computational consequences of losing convexity in PtO. Further specialization of the PtO-KRR solver might improve its computational efficiency, but would require additional algorithmic effort.

As shown in Table 6.3.2, increasing dyd_{y} substantially raises online computation, whereas relative decision performance varies comparatively little over the tested range. In particular, GtO’s relative cost stays above 0.91 as dyd_{y} increases from 1 to 15; the experiment does not exhibit a crossover favoring PtO. Similar stability of PtO performance with respect to outcome dimension has been reported by Bertsimas and Koduri (2022). Here, increasing dyd_{y} also enlarges the placement and recourse problems, so the runtime changes capture more than the cost of learning higher-dimensional uncertainty. Over the tested range, outcome dimension has a more pronounced effect on computation than on the relative decision-performance ranking.

6.4 Real Case Study: Fresh Retail Inventory

We compare PtO and GtO in a fresh-retail inventory setting using the FreshRetailNet-LT dataset released by Dingdong Fresh (Wang et al. 2025).11 1 https://huggingface.co/datasets/Dingdong-Inc/FreshRetailNet-LT The application combines several features common in operational decision making: demand varies across locations and operating conditions, stockouts censor observed sales, and contextual information includes both continuous and categorical variables. It therefore provides an opportunity to examine the usefulness of the two approaches beyond the setting of our theoretical analysis and to assess whether similar insights emerge with real operational data.

6.4.1 Data and Experimental Design.

FreshRetailNet-LT contains daily sales records for 576 perishable products across 1,057 stores in 18 major Chinese cities. We focus on product 156 because of its broad store coverage and long sales history, and select the 50 stores with the longest common observation period. These stores span 11 cities and are observed from June 5, 2023 to July 20, 2025, yielding a balanced panel of 777 days and 38,850 store-day observations.

Stockouts occur in approximately 20% of the observations and may censor sales. We apply the TimesNet-based demand recovery procedure described by Wang et al. (2025) to the hourly sales and stock-status data, then aggregate recovered demand to daily totals for training and evaluation. Since procurement costs and actual selling prices are unavailable, we normalize the unit overage cost to one and specify the shortage penalty as b⁡(x)=4​((discount⁡(x)−0.7)/0.3)+b(x)=4((\operatorname{discount}(x)-0.7)/0.3)^{+}, where discount⁡(x)\operatorname{discount}(x) denotes the ratio of the discounted selling price to the regular price, which is included as a covariate in the dataset. The resulting inventory problem is

minz≥0⁡𝔼⁡[(z−Y)++b⁡(X)​(Y−z)+∣X=x0].\min_{z\geq 0}\;\mathbb{E}\left[(z-Y)^{+}+b(X)(Y-z)^{+}\mid X=x_{0}\right].

This penalty makes shortages more costly when the product sells closer to its regular price. The evaluation therefore measures decision performance using recovered demand and a specified cost function.

We construct 37 exogenous features from store location, calendar effects, promotions, discounts, and weather. City, weekday, and month use one-hot encoding; holidays and promotional activity use binary indicators; the remaining features are continuous. Following Ban and Rudin (2019), we also incorporate the preceding 14 days of demand, summarized by their sample mean and the 13 differences between consecutive order statistics (Liyanage and Shanthikumar 2005). The resulting covariate vector has 51 components: 32 binary or one-hot indicators and 19 continuous variables.

All settings use the same chronological split. After the initial 14-day history window, training runs from June 19, 2023 to March 22, 2025, validation covers March 23–April 13, 2025, and testing covers April 14–July 20, 2025. Each store contributes 643 training days, 22 validation days, and 98 test days.

We consider three store settings to examine how the comparison changes as learning expands from a single location to a broader network. This reflects a practical modeling choice for retailers: whether to build a model using one store’s history or pool observations across stores. Pooling provides more training data but also introduces greater heterogeneity. The one-store setting uses the highest-sales store among the 50 selected stores; the 11-store setting uses the highest-sales store in each city; and the 50-store setting uses all selected stores. Their respective training samples contain 643, 7,073, and 32,150 observations. These settings allow us to examine the joint effects of data availability and pooling scope, rather than isolate a sample-size effect.

This application extends beyond the continuous-covariate setting of our theoretical analysis because the contextual features include both continuous and categorical variables. We therefore use learning models that accommodate these mixed feature types. For GtO, we use TabCSDI (Zheng and Charoenphakdee 2022), a diffusion model for mixed-type tabular data, to generate conditional demand scenarios. For PtO, we add random forests (RF) to the existing surface-fitting benchmarks. For KRR, details of incorporating one-hot-encoded categorical variables into the kernel are provided in Appendix 10.3. The subsequent optimization steps remain unchanged. The purpose is to examine whether the two approaches remain useful with learning models suited to the application and whether the tradeoffs identified earlier persist beyond the assumptions of the theory. Hyperparameters are selected using validation decision cost, as in the preceding experiments.

Because the true conditional demand distribution is unavailable, we evaluate each method using its average realized cost on the test set, computed from recovered demand. For method MM and store setting ss, we report normalized cost C~M,s=C¯M,s/C¯SAA,s\widetilde{C}_{M,s}=\overline{C}_{M,s}/\overline{C}_{\mathrm{SAA},s}. SAA consequently has normalized cost one, and lower values indicate better performance.

6.4.2 Decision Quality and Online Computation.

Panel A of Table 6.4.2 shows that the relative performance of PtO and GtO changes across the pooling settings. With one store, PtO-RF achieves the lowest normalized cost, 0.4134, followed by PtO-KRR at 0.4509. GtO improves on SAA but performs worse than every PtO benchmark, with a normalized cost of 0.8324. With 11 stores, GtO achieves 0.4752 compared with 0.5106 for RF, the best PtO benchmark, reducing cost by approximately 6.9%. With 50 stores, GtO achieves 0.5006 compared with 0.5512 for PtO-KRR, a reduction of approximately 9.2%.

The shift toward GtO with broader pooling resembles the sample-size pattern in the synthetic experiments. However, because pooling changes both the training sample and the store population, the performance differences across settings cannot be attributed to sample size alone.

Panel B reports the computational tradeoff. GtO’s online time increases from 1.05 seconds in the one-store setting to 7.13 seconds with 11 stores and 18.09 seconds with 50 stores. All PtO methods remain below 0.11 seconds in the three settings. With 50 stores, for example, GtO’s 9.2% cost reduction relative to PtO-KRR accompanies an online time of 18.09 seconds, compared with 0.030 seconds for PtO-KRR. Thus, PtO performs better in the smallest setting on both decision quality and latency, while broader pooling introduces a tradeoff between GtO’s lower decision cost and PtO’s faster response. These findings extend the empirical comparison to mixed contextual features and recovered demand, while illustrating similar tradeoffs between data availability, decision quality, and computation.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we study a fundamental representation choice in contextual stochastic optimization: should one learn the conditional objective needed for a particular decision problem, or learn the underlying conditional distribution and generate scenarios for subsequent optimization? We formalize these two approaches as Predict-then-Optimize (PtO) and Generate-then-Optimize (GtO). Our main message is that neither paradigm is uniformly preferable. PtO benefits from statistical parsimony and avoids online scenario generation, whereas GtO learns a richer stochastic representation that can preserve the structure of the downstream optimization problem and be reused across decision tasks. The appropriate choice therefore depends on the statistical, computational, and operational characteristics of the problem.

Our theoretical analysis makes this trade-off explicit for convex contextual stochastic optimization. For a broad class of local PtO methods, nonnegative weighting preserves the convexity of the original problem but limits the ability of the estimator to exploit high-order smoothness in high-dimensional contexts. Global PtO methods such as KRR can achieve greater statistical efficiency by exploiting smoothness, but their signed weights need not preserve convexity. GtO avoids this tension because its downstream problem is an ordinary sample average approximation with nonnegative scenario weights and therefore inherits the convexity of the primitive stochastic program. Its statistical performance, however, depends on learning the richer conditional distribution. We then decompose the regret of GtO into an offline learning error and an online optimization error, providing a framework for directly comparing its statistical efficiency with that of PtO.

These results lead to a practical characterization of when each paradigm is attractive. PtO tends to be preferable when the conditional objective is sufficiently smooth, the uncertainty dimension is large, offline data are limited, the downstream task is stable, or online computation is particularly costly. GtO becomes more attractive when the conditional distribution is substantially smoother than the induced objective, the context dimension is large relative to the uncertainty dimension, preserving the structure of downstream optimization is important, sufficient training data are available, or the learned uncertainty model is intended to support multiple decision problems. Our numerical and empirical studies complement the theoretical analysis by illustrating how data availability, covariate dimension, learning formulation, and downstream problem structure affect the relative decision quality and online computational costs of PtO and GtO.

This study leaves several directions for future research. First, our analysis focuses on convex contextual stochastic optimization; extending the comparison to nonconvex, discrete, and multistage decision problems may reveal different trade-offs between statistical representation and optimization structure. Second, both PtO and GtO in this paper follow a sequential learning and optimization paradigm. An important direction is to study the predictive vs. generative representation choice within integrated or decision-focused learning frameworks. Third, reducing the online computational cost of GtO through faster conditional generators, more efficient scenario construction, or adaptive sampling may further expand the range of settings in which generative decision making is practically attractive. More broadly, this paper hopes that viewing contextual decision making through the choice of what statistical object to learn provides a useful perspective for designing data-driven optimization methods.

Appendix

8 Proofs in Section 3

In this section, we prove Proposition 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 respectively.

8.1 Proof of Proposition 3.1

To analyze the regret ℛn​(x0)\mathcal{R}_{n}(x_{0}), we adopt the decomposition

ℛn​(x0)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{n}(x_{0})
=[h⁡(z^n​(x0),x0)−h^n​(z^n​(x0),x0)]+[h^n​(z^n​(x0),x0)−h^n​(z∗​(x0),x0)]+[h^n​(z∗​(x0),x0)−h⁡(z∗​(x0),x0)]\displaystyle\,=\,\left[h(\hat{z}_{n}(x_{0});x_{0})-\hat{h}_{n}(\hat{z}_{n}(x_{0});x_{0})\right]+\left[\hat{h}_{n}(\hat{z}_{n}(x_{0});x_{0})-\hat{h}_{n}(z^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})\right]+\left[\hat{h}_{n}(z^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})-h(z^{\ast}(x_{0});x_{0})\right]
≤ 2​supz∈𝒵|h⁡(z,x0)−h^n​(z,x0)|.\displaystyle\,\leq\,2\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\absolutevalue{h(z;x_0) -\hat{h}_n(z;x_0)}. (18)

Equation (18) shows that controlling the regret of the weighted PtO procedure reduces to bounding the approximation error between the estimated conditional objective h^n\hat{h}_{n} and the true conditional objective hh, uniformly over 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. For each fixed decision z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, h^n​(z,⋅)\hat{h}_{n}(z;\cdot) is the KRR estimator of h⁡(z,⋅)h(z;\cdot), constructed using the observed costs c⁡(z,Xi,Yi)c(z;X_{i},Y_{i}) as regression responses. We therefore begin by analyzing the KRR estimation error for a fixed decision and then extend the resulting bound uniformly over the decision set.

For a fixed decision z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, define the observed cost, its conditional mean, and the centered observation noise by

Uz,i:=c⁡(z,Xi,Yi),hz​(x):=h⁡(z,x)=𝔼⁡[Uz,i∣Xi=x],ξz,i:=Uz,i−hz​(Xi).U_{z,i}:=c(z;X_{i},Y_{i}),\qquad h_{z}(x):=h(z;x)=\mathbb{E}\left[U_{z,i}\mid X_{i}=x\right],\qquad\xi_{z,i}:=U_{z,i}-h_{z}(X_{i}).

Then, Uz,i=hz​(Xi)+ξz,i​ and ​𝔼​[ξz,i∣Xi]=0.U_{z,i}=h_{z}(X_{i})+\xi_{z,i}\text{ and }\mathbb{E}[\xi_{z,i}\mid X_{i}]=0. Moreover, Assumption 2 gives |Uz,i|≤M|U_{z,i}|\leq M and |hz​(Xi)|≤M|h_{z}(X_{i})|\leq M, and hence |ξz,i|≤2​M|\xi_{z,i}|\leq 2M. Therefore, by Hoeffding’s lemma,

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(t​ξz,i)|Xi]≤exp⁡(2​M2​t2),t∈ℝ.\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(t\xi_{z,i})\,\middle|\,X_{i}\right]\leq\exp(2M^2t^2),\quad t\in\mathbb{R}. (19)

Thus, conditional on X1:nX_{1:n}, the noise variables ξz,1,…,ξz,n\xi_{z,1},\ldots,\xi_{z,n} are independent, mean-zero, and sub-Gaussian with a sub-Gaussian bound independent of zz.

To separate the effect of observation noise from the remaining estimation error, we consider the conditional expectation of the KRR estimator given the observed covariates. Define h¯n,z(x):=𝔼[h^n(z;x)|X1:n]\bar{h}_{n,z}(x):=\mathbb{E}[\hat{h}_{n}(z;x)|X_{1:n}]. Let 𝐜(z;X1:n,Y1:n)=(c(z;X1,Y1),…,c(z;Xn,Yn))⊤\mathbf{c}(z;X_{1:n},Y_{1:n})=(c(z;X_{1},Y_{1}),\ldots,c(z;X_{n},Y_{n}))^{\top} denote the vector of observed responses. By Equation (4), the KRR estimator admits the closed-form expression

h^n(z;x)=kn(x)⊤(Kn+nλnIn)−1𝐜(z,X1:n,Y1:n).\hat{h}_{n}(z;x)=k_{n}(x)^{\top}(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}\mathbf{c}(z,X_{1:n},Y_{1:n}).

Since KnK_{n} and kn​(x)k_{n}(x) are determined by X1:nX_{1:n} and 𝔼[𝐜(z,X1:n,Y1:n)|X1:n]=(hz(X1),…,hz(Xn))⊤\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{c}(z,X_{1:n},Y_{1:n})|X_{1:n}]=(h_{z}(X_{1}),\ldots,h_{z}(X_{n}))^{\top}, taking the conditional expectation gives

h¯n,z​(x)=kn​(x)⊤​(Kn+n​λn​In)−1​(hz​(X1),…,hz​(Xn))⊤.\bar{h}_{n,z}(x)=k_{n}(x)^{\top}(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}(h_{z}(X_{1}),\ldots,h_{z}(X_{n}))^{\top}.

Thus, h¯n,z\bar{h}_{n,z} coincides with the KRR estimator fitted to the noiseless responses hz​(X1),…,hz​(Xn)h_{z}(X_{1}),\ldots,h_{z}(X_{n}). We therefore decompose the objective approximation error as

‖h^n(z;⋅)−hz‖∞≤‖h^n​(z,⋅)−h¯n,z‖∞⏟=:Sn,z+‖h¯n,z−hz‖∞⏟=:Bn,z.\left\|\hat{h}_{n}(z;\cdot)-h_{z}\right\|_{\infty}\leq\underbrace{\left\|\hat{h}_{n}(z;\cdot)-\bar{h}_{n,z}\right\|_{\infty}}_{=:S_{n,z}}+\underbrace{\left\|\bar{h}_{n,z}-h_{z}\right\|_{\infty}}_{=:B_{n,z}}. (20)

The first term Sn,zS_{n,z} is the stochastic error arising from the observation noise, while the second term Bn,zB_{n,z} is the conditional bias. We first establish a bound for Sn,zS_{n,z} on a high-probability event for the random design X1:nX_{1:n} in Lemma 8.1. We then bound Bn,zB_{n,z} on the same event and combine the two bounds to obtain a fixed-decision sup-norm error bound in Lemma 8.4. Finally, Lemma 8.6 extends this result uniformly over 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and establishes the expected uniform approximation error needed to control the regret.

Let d:=dxd:=d_{x}. For a given realization X1:nX_{1:n}, define the empirical norm ‖f‖n:=(n−1​∑i=1nf​(Xi)2)1/2\|f\|_{n}:=(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(X_{i})^{2})^{1/2}. For a t≥1t\geq 1, define the event

ℰn(t):={∥f∥L2≤max{C1∥f∥n,C2tn−s/d∥f∥Hs} for all f∈Hs(𝒳)},\mathcal{E}_{n}(t):=\left\{\|f\|_{L^{2}}\leq\max\left\{C_{1}\|f\|_{n},\,C_{2}tn^{-s/d}\|f\|_{H^{s}}\right\}\text{ for all }f\in H^{s}(\mathcal{X})\right\},

where C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are the constants in Theorem S4.1 in the Supplementary Material of Tuo and Zou (2026).

Lemma 8.1 (Sn,zS_{n,z} bound on a good-design event)

Suppose the conditions of Proposition 3.1 hold. Then, for any fixed A>0A>0, there exist constants CA′>0C_{A}^{\prime}>0, CA<∞C_{A}<\infty, and an integer NA≥1N_{A}\geq 1, all independent of nn and zz, such that the following two statements hold for every n≥NAn\geq N_{A}. (i) Let tn:=CA′​(log⁡n)s/dt_{n}:=C_{A}^{\prime}(\log n)^{s/d}. The event ℰn​(tn)\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}) holds with a large probability,

ℙ⁡(ℰn​(tn)c)≤12​n−A.\mathbb{P}\bigl(\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n})^{c}\bigr)\,\leq\,\frac{1}{2}n^{-A}. (21)

(ii) For every z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} and every realization X1:n∈ℰn(tn)X_{1:n}\in\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}),

ℙ(Sn,z>CAn−1/2λn−d4​slog⁡n|X1:n)≤12n−A.\mathbb{P}\left(S_{n,z}>C_{A}n^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-\frac{d}{4s}}\sqrt{\log n}\,\middle|\,X_{1:n}\right)\,\leq\,\frac{1}{2}n^{-A}. (22)

The proof of Lemma 8.1 relies on the smoothing-regime bound in Lemma S5.1 in the Supplementary Material of Tuo and Zou (2026). Applying this bound in our setting requires verifying several conditions. To make these conditions explicit and the subsequent argument easier to follow, we first restate Lemma S5.1 of Tuo and Zou (2026) in our notation as Lemma 8.2.

Lemma 8.2 (Lemma S5.1 of Tuo and Zou 2026)

Let g∈ℋνg\in\mathcal{H}_{\nu} and g^\hat{g} be the KRR estimator fitted to the responses g⁡(X1),…,g⁡(Xn)g(X_{1}),\ldots,g(X_{n}) with regularization parameter λn>0\lambda_{n}>0. Suppose there exist constants Cg>0C_{g}>0 and δ∈(0,1]\delta\in(0,1] such that

|⟨g,f⟩ℋν|≤Cg​‖f‖L2δ​‖f‖ℋν1−δfor all ​f∈ℋν.|\langle g,f\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}|\,\leq\,C_{g}\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{\delta}\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}^{1-\delta}\quad\text{for all }f\in\mathcal{H}_{\nu}. (23)

Suppose further that the design X1:nX_{1:n} satisfies ‖f‖L2≤max⁡{a​‖f‖n,b​‖f‖ℋν}​ for all ​f∈ℋν\|f\|_{L^{2}}\leq\max\{a\|f\|_{n},\,b\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}\}\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{H}_{\nu} and for some constants a,b>0a,b>0 satisfying b≤a​λn1/2b\leq a\lambda_{n}^{1/2}. Then

‖g^−g‖n≤ 2​Cg​aδ​λn(1+δ)/2.\|\hat{g}-g\|_{n}\,\leq\,2C_{g}a^{\delta}\lambda_{n}^{(1+\delta)/2}. (24)

With Lemma 8.2 in place, we now prove Lemma 8.1.

Proof 8.3

Proof of Lemma 8.1 Under Assumption 2, Theorem S4.1 of Tuo and Zou (2026) implies that there exist constants C1,C2,C3,C4>0C_{1},C_{2},C_{3},C_{4}>0, independent of nn and the design points, such that for every t≥1t\geq 1, ℙ⁡(ℰn​(t)c)≤C3​exp⁡{−C4​td/s}.\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{n}(t)^{c})\leq C_{3}\exp\{-C_{4}t^{d/s}\}. Therefore, ℙ⁡(ℰn​(tn)c)≤12​n−A,\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n})^{c})\leq\frac{1}{2}n^{-A}, which establishes Equation (21) for all n≥NAn\geq N_{A}.

We next prove Equation (22). We follow the argument in the proof of Theorem S2.3 of Tuo and Zou (2026), particularly their Equations (S5.61)–(S5.62), to bound the stochastic error Sn,zS_{n,z}. For each fixed z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, define the stochastic process 𝔾n,z​(x):=h^n​(z,x)−h¯n,z​(x)\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x):=\hat{h}_{n}(z;x)-\bar{h}_{n,z}(x), indexed by x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}. Then Sn,z=supx∈𝒳|𝔾n,z​(x)|.S_{n,z}=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}|\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x)|. Fix any x0∈𝒳x_{0}\in\mathcal{X}. By the triangle inequality,

Sn,z≤supx∈𝒳|𝔾n,z​(x)−𝔾n,z​(x0)|+|𝔾n,z​(x0)|.S_{n,z}\,\leq\,\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}|\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x)-\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x_{0})|+|\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x_{0})|. (25)

In the following, we bound the two terms in the right hand side of Equation (25) separately. For the first term, we equip 𝒳\mathcal{X} with a semimetric that controls the increments of 𝔾n,z\mathbb{G}_{n,z} and apply a generic chaining inequality of Dirksen (2015). The second term is controlled directly using a sub-Gaussian tail bound.

Now we bound the first term in Equation (25). Conditional on X1:nX_{1:n}, the process 𝔾n,z\mathbb{G}_{n,z} is centered. Let 𝛏z:=(ξz,1,…,ξz,n)⊤\bm{\xi}_{z}:=(\xi_{z,1},\ldots,\xi_{z,n})^{\top} denote the noise vector defined above. By the closed-form KRR representation and Uz,i=hz​(Xi)+ξz,iU_{z,i}=h_{z}(X_{i})+\xi_{z,i}, we have 𝔾n,z​(x)=kn​(x)⊤​(Kn+n​λn​In)−1​𝛏z.\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x)=k_{n}(x)^{\top}(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}\bm{\xi}_{z}. We now construct a semimetric using the KRR representation. For each x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, define the kernel section ϕx​(⋅):=Kν​(⋅,x)\phi_{x}(\cdot):=K_{\nu}(\cdot,x), and let ϕ^x\hat{\phi}_{x} denote the KRR estimator fitted to the responses ϕx​(X1),…,ϕx​(Xn)\phi_{x}(X_{1}),\ldots,\phi_{x}(X_{n}). Since ϕx(X1:n)=kn(x)\phi_{x}(X_{1:n})=k_{n}(x), the closed-form KRR representation gives ϕ^x(⋅)=kn(x)⊤(Kn+nλnIn)−1Kν(⋅,X1:n)⊤.\hat{\phi}_{x}(\cdot)=k_{n}(x)^{\top}(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}K_{\nu}(\cdot,X_{1:n})^{\top}. Evaluating at the training points and subtracting ϕx(X1:n)=kn(x)\phi_{x}(X_{1:n})=k_{n}(x) yields

(ϕ^x−ϕx)(X1:n)=[Kn(Kn+nλnIn)−1−In]kn(x)=−nλn(Kn+nλnIn)−1kn(x).(\hat{\phi}_{x}-\phi_{x})(X_{1:n})\,=\,\left[K_{n}(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}-I_{n}\right]k_{n}(x)\,=\,-n\lambda_{n}(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}k_{n}(x).

Consequently, 𝔾n,z(x)=−1n​λn∑i=1n(ϕ^x−ϕx)(Xi)ξz,i.\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x)=-\frac{1}{n\lambda_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{\phi}_{x}-\phi_{x})(X_{i})\xi_{z,i}. For x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}, define ϕx,x′:=ϕx−ϕx′\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}:=\phi_{x}-\phi_{x^{\prime}} and ϕ^x,x′:=ϕ^x−ϕ^x′\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}:=\hat{\phi}_{x}-\hat{\phi}_{x^{\prime}}. Then

𝔾n,z(x)−𝔾n,z(x′)=−1n​λn∑i=1n(ϕ^x,x′−ϕx,x′)(Xi)ξz,i.\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x)-\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x^{\prime})\,=\,-\frac{1}{n\lambda_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}-\phi_{x,x^{\prime}})(X_{i})\xi_{z,i}. (26)

Since the noise variables ξz,i\xi_{z,i} are conditionally independent and sub-Gaussian, the conditional fluctuations of these increments in Equation (26) are controlled by ‖ϕ^x,x′−ϕx,x′‖n\|\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}-\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}\|_{n}. We therefore define the following semimetric on 𝒳\mathcal{X} to control the increments of 𝔾n,z\mathbb{G}_{n,z}:

𝔡n(x,x′):= 22Mλn−1n−1/2∥ϕ^x,x′−ϕx,x′∥n.\mathfrak{d}_{n}(x,x^{\prime})\,:=\,2\sqrt{2}M\lambda_{n}^{-1}n^{-1/2}\|\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}-\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}\|_{n}. (27)

This is a semimetric on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. By Equation (19) and the conditional independence of ξz,1,…,ξz,n\xi_{z,1},\ldots,\xi_{z,n},

𝔼[exp{θ(𝔾n,z(x)−𝔾n,z(x′))}|X1:n]≤exp{2​M2​θ2n​λn2‖ϕ^x,x′−ϕx,x′‖n2}=exp{θ2​𝔡n2​(x,x′)4}.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left\{\theta\bigl(\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x)-\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x^{\prime})\bigr)\right\}\,\middle|\,X_{1:n}\right]\,\leq\,\exp\left\{\frac{2M^{2}\theta^{2}}{n\lambda_{n}^{2}}\left\|\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}-\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}\right\|_{n}^{2}\right\}\,=\,\exp\left\{\frac{\theta^{2}\mathfrak{d}_{n}^{2}(x,x^{\prime})}{4}\right\}.

A Chernoff bound therefore yields

ℙ(|𝔾n,z(x)−𝔾n,z(x′)|≥u𝔡n(x,x′)|X1:n)≤ 2e−u2,u≥0.\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x)-\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x^{\prime})\right|\geq u\,\mathfrak{d}_{n}(x,x^{\prime})\,\middle|\,X_{1:n}\right)\,\leq\,2e^{-u^{2}},\quad u\geq 0.

In the terminology of Dirksen (2015), a stochastic process {Xt:t∈T}\{X_{t}:t\in T\} is a ψ2\psi_{2}-process with respect to a semimetric ρ\rho if its increments satisfy ℙ⁡(|Xt−Xs|≥u​ρ​(t,s))≤2​e−u2​ for all ​s,t∈T,u≥0.\mathbb{P}\left(|X_{t}-X_{s}|\geq u\,\rho(t,s)\right)\leq 2e^{-u^{2}}\text{ for all }s,t\in T,u\geq 0. This verifies the conditions required for Theorem 3.2 of Dirksen (2015). Applying that theorem, we get a generic chaining inequality for the increment of the stochastic process {𝔾n,z​(x):x∈𝒳}\{\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x):x\in\mathcal{X}\}. That is, for any fixed x0∈𝒳x_{0}\in\mathcal{X} and every u≥1u\geq 1,

We first bound the diameter Δ𝔡n​(𝒳)\Delta_{\mathfrak{d}_{n}}(\mathcal{X}). Recall that ϕx​(⋅)=Kν​(⋅,x)\phi_{x}(\cdot)=K_{\nu}(\cdot,x). ∥f∥L2≤max{C1∥f∥n,C~2tnn−s/d∥f∥ℋν},f∈ℋν,\|f\|_{L^{2}}\,\leq\,\max\left\{C_{1}\|f\|_{n},\,\widetilde{C}_{2}t_{n}n^{-s/d}\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}\right\},\quad f\in\mathcal{H}_{\nu},

for some constant C~2>0\widetilde{C}_{2}>0. Since tnn−s/d=o(λn1/2)t_{n}n^{-s/d}=o(\lambda_{n}^{1/2}), we have C~2tnn−s/d≤C1λn1/2\widetilde{C}_{2}t_{n}n^{-s/d}\leq C_{1}\lambda_{n}^{1/2} for all sufficiently large nn. Hence, the conditions of Lemma 8.2 are satisfied. Applying that lemma, we obtain

‖ϕ^x−ϕx‖n≤C​λn1−d4​s\|\hat{\phi}_{x}-\phi_{x}\|_{n}\,\leq\,C\lambda_{n}^{1-\frac{d}{4s}} (30)

uniformly over x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}. For any x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}, ϕ^x,x′−ϕx,x′=(ϕ^x−ϕx)−(ϕ^x′−ϕx′),\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}-\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}=(\hat{\phi}_{x}-\phi_{x})-(\hat{\phi}_{x^{\prime}}-\phi_{x^{\prime}}), and hence, by Equation (30),

‖ϕ^x,x′−ϕx,x′‖n≤C​λn1−d4​s.\left\|\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}-\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}\right\|_{n}\,\leq\,C\lambda_{n}^{1-\frac{d}{4s}}. (31)

Substituting this bound into Equation (27) yields 𝔡n(x,x′)≤Cn−1/2λn−d4​s\mathfrak{d}_{n}(x,x^{\prime})\leq Cn^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-\frac{d}{4s}} uniformly over x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}. Therefore,

Δ𝔡n(𝒳)≤Cn−1/2λn−d4​s.\Delta_{\mathfrak{d}_{n}}(\mathcal{X})\,\leq\,Cn^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-\frac{d}{4s}}. (32)

We next bound γ2​(𝒳,𝔡n)\gamma_{2}(\mathcal{X},\mathfrak{d}_{n}). Fix any τ∈(0,min⁡{ν,1})\tau\in(0,\min\{\nu,1\}). Since s=ν+d/2s=\nu+d/2, the Sobolev embedding and the norm equivalence between ℋν\mathcal{H}_{\nu} and Hs​(𝒳)H^{s}(\mathcal{X}) imply that

|f(x)−f(x′)|≤C∥f∥ℋν∥x−x′∥τ,f∈ℋν,x,x′∈𝒳.|f(x)-f(x^{\prime})|\,\leq\,C\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}\|x-x^{\prime}\|^{\tau},\quad f\in\mathcal{H}_{\nu},~x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}.

By the reproducing property,

‖ϕx,x′‖ℋν=sup‖f‖ℋν≤1|⟨ϕx,x′,f⟩ℋν|=sup‖f‖ℋν≤1|f⁡(x)−f⁡(x′)|≤C​‖x−x′‖τ.\|\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}\,=\,\sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}\leq 1}|\langle\phi_{x,x^{\prime}},f\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}|\,=\,\sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}\leq 1}|f(x)-f(x^{\prime})|\,\leq\,C\|x-x^{\prime}\|^{\tau}.

Since ϕ^x,x′\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}} is the KRR estimator fitted to the responses ϕx,x′​(X1),…,ϕx,x′​(Xn)\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}(X_{1}),\ldots,\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}(X_{n}), comparing its regularized empirical objective with that of ϕx,x′\phi_{x,x^{\prime}} gives ‖ϕ^x,x′−ϕx,x′‖n2+λn​‖ϕ^x,x′‖ℋν2≤λn​‖ϕx,x′‖ℋν2.\|\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}-\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}\|_{n}^{2}+\lambda_{n}\|\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}^{2}\leq\lambda_{n}\|\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}^{2}. Consequently, ‖ϕ^x,x′−ϕx,x′‖n≤C​λn1/2​‖x−x′‖τ.\|\hat{\phi}_{x,x^{\prime}}-\phi_{x,x^{\prime}}\|_{n}\leq C\lambda_{n}^{1/2}\|x-x^{\prime}\|^{\tau}. Substituting this bound into Equation (27) yields

𝔡n(x,x′)≤Cn−1/2λn−1/2∥x−x′∥τ,x,x′∈𝒳.\mathfrak{d}_{n}(x,x^{\prime})\,\leq\,Cn^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-1/2}\|x-x^{\prime}\|^{\tau},\quad x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}. (33)

By Equation (33), any Euclidean cover of 𝒳\mathcal{X} with radius rε:=(ε/(Cn−1/2λn−1/2))1/τr_{\varepsilon}:=(\varepsilon/(Cn^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-1/2}))^{1/\tau} is also an ε\varepsilon-cover under 𝔡n\mathfrak{d}_{n}. Hence, N(𝒳,𝔡n,ε)≤N(𝒳,∥⋅∥,rε).N(\mathcal{X},\mathfrak{d}_{n},\varepsilon)\leq N(\mathcal{X},\|\cdot\|,r_{\varepsilon}). Since 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a bounded subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, the standard Euclidean covering number bound gives

logN(𝒳,𝔡n,ε)≤dlog[1+C((n−1/2λn−1/2)/ε)1/τ].\log N(\mathcal{X},\mathfrak{d}_{n},\varepsilon)\,\leq\,d\log\left[1+C\left((n^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-1/2})/\varepsilon\right)^{1/\tau}\right]. (34)

For convenience, let an:=n−1/2λn−d/(4s)a_{n}:=n^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-d/(4s)} and bn:=n−1/2λn−1/2b_{n}:=n^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-1/2}. Combining Equations (29), (32), and (34), we obtain

γ2​(𝒳,𝔡n)\displaystyle\gamma_{2}(\mathcal{X},\mathfrak{d}_{n}) ≤C​∫0C​an(log⁡[1+C​(bn/ε)1/τ])1/2​𝑑ε≤C​an​∫01(log⁡[1+C​(bn/(an​v))1/τ])1/2​𝑑v\displaystyle\leq\,C\int_{0}^{Ca_{n}}\left({\log\left[1+C\left({b_{n}}/{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/\tau}\right]}\right)^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon\,\leq\,Ca_{n}\int_{0}^{1}\left({\log\left[1+C\left({b_{n}}/({a_{n}v})\right)^{1/\tau}\right]}\right)^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}v
≤C​an​∫01(log⁡[1+C​(bn/an)1/τ]+1τ​log⁡(1/v))1/2​𝑑v\displaystyle\leq\,Ca_{n}\int_{0}^{1}\left({\log\left[1+C\left({b_{n}}/{a_{n}}\right)^{1/\tau}\right]+\frac{1}{\tau}\log(1/v)}\right)^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}v
≤C​an​∫01[(log⁡[1+C​(bn/an)1/τ])1/2+(1τ​log⁡(1/v))1/2]​𝑑v\displaystyle\leq\,Ca_{n}\int_{0}^{1}\left[\left({\log\left[1+C\left({b_{n}}/{a_{n}}\right)^{1/\tau}\right]}\right)^{1/2}+\left(\frac{1}{{\tau}}{\log(1/v)}\right)^{1/2}\right]\mathrm{d}v
=C​an​[(log⁡(1+C​λn−ν2​s​τ))1/2+π2​τ]\displaystyle=\,Ca_{n}\left[\left({\log\left(1+C\lambda_{n}^{-\frac{\nu}{2s\tau}}\right)}\right)^{1/2}+\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{\tau}}\right]
≤C​an​[log⁡(1+C)+ν2​s​τ​log⁡(1/λn)+π2​τ]≤C​an​log⁡(C′/λn).\displaystyle\leq\,Ca_{n}\left[\sqrt{\log(1+C)+\frac{\nu}{2s\tau}\log(1/\lambda_n)}+\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{\tau}}\right]\,\leq\,Ca_{n}\sqrt{\log(C'/\lambda_n)}.

In the preceding inequalities, C>0C>0 denotes a generic constant that may differ from one occurrence to another but is independent of nn, zz, and the design points. The last inequality holds for all sufficiently large nn, since λn→0\lambda_{n}\to 0 and τ>0\tau>0 is fixed. Therefore,

γ2(𝒳,𝔡n)≤Cn−1/2λn−d4​slog⁡(C′/λn).\gamma_{2}(\mathcal{X},\mathfrak{d}_{n})\,\leq\,Cn^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-\frac{d}{4s}}\sqrt{\log(C'/\lambda_n)}. (35)

Fix any x0∈𝒳x_{0}\in\mathcal{X}. Substituting Equations (32) and (35) into Equation (28), we obtain, for every realization X1:n∈ℰn(tn)X_{1:n}\in\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}) and every u≥1u\geq 1,

ℙ(supx∈𝒳|𝔾n,z(x)−𝔾n,z(x0)|>Cn−1/2λn−d4​s[log⁡(C′/λn)+u]|X1:n)≤e−c​u2,\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\left|\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x)-\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x_{0})\right|>Cn^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-\frac{d}{4s}}\left[\sqrt{\log(C'/\lambda_n)}+u\right]\,\middle|\,X_{1:n}\right)\,\leq\,e^{-cu^{2}}, (36)

where c,C>0c,C>0 are independent of zz.

𝔼[exp{θ𝔾n,z(x0)}|X1:n]≤exp{2​M2​θ2n​λn2∥ϕ^x0−ϕx0∥n2}.\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left\{\theta\mathbb{G}_{n,z}(x_{0})\right\}\,\middle|\,X_{1:n}\right]\,\leq\,\exp\left\{\frac{2M^{2}\theta^{2}}{n\lambda_{n}^{2}}\|\hat{\phi}_{x_{0}}-\phi_{x_{0}}\|_{n}^{2}\right\}.

Equations  (25),  (36) and (37), together with a union bound, imply that for every realization X1:n∈ℰn(tn)X_{1:n}\in\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}) and every u≥1u\geq 1,

ℙ(Sn,z>Cn−1/2λn−d4​s[log⁡(C′/λn)+u]|X1:n)≤ 3e−c​u2.\mathbb{P}\left(S_{n,z}>Cn^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-\frac{d}{4s}}\left[\sqrt{\log(C'/\lambda_n)}+u\right]\,\middle|\,X_{1:n}\right)\,\leq\,3e^{-cu^{2}}. (38)

ℙ(Sn,z>CAn−1/2λn−d4​slog⁡n|X1:n)≤12n−A\mathbb{P}\left(S_{n,z}>C_{A}n^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-\frac{d}{4s}}\sqrt{\log n}\,\middle|\,X_{1:n}\right)\,\leq\,\frac{1}{2}n^{-A}

for every realization X1:n∈ℰn(tn)X_{1:n}\in\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}) and all sufficiently large nn. Together with Equation (21), this proves the two assertions of Lemma 8.1. □\square

Having established a bound for the stochastic error Sn,zS_{n,z} on the good-design event ℰn​(tn)\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}), we next control the conditional bias Bn,zB_{n,z} on the same event and combine the two bounds to yield the fixed-decision sup-norm result in Lemma 8.4.

Lemma 8.4 (Fixed-decision sup-norm bound for KRR)

Suppose the conditions of Proposition 3.1 hold. Then, for every fixed A>0A>0, there exist constants CA<∞C_{A}<\infty and nA<∞n_{A}<\infty, independent of zz, such that for all n≥nAn\geq n_{A} and all z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z},

ℙ𝒟n​(‖h^n​(z,⋅)−h⁡(z,⋅)‖∞>CA​(log⁡nn)ν2​ν+dx)≤n−A.\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{D}_{n}}\left(\left\|\hat{h}_{n}(z;\cdot)-h(z;\cdot)\right\|_{\infty}>C_{A}\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\frac{\nu}{2\nu+d_{x}}}\right)\,\leq\,n^{-A}. (39)
Proof 8.5

Proof of Lemma 8.4

Recall that d=dxd=d_{x} and s=ν+d/2s=\nu+d/2. By Assumption 3.2 and the norm equivalence between ℋν\mathcal{H}_{\nu} and Hs​(𝒳)H^{s}(\mathcal{X}), there exists a constant Bℋ<∞B_{\mathcal{H}}<\infty, independent of zz, such that

supz∈𝒵‖hz‖ℋν≤Bℋ.\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\|h_{z}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}\,\leq\,B_{\mathcal{H}}. (40)

Conditional on X1:nX_{1:n}, h¯n,z\bar{h}_{n,z} is the KRR estimator based on the responses hz​(X1),…,hz​(Xn)h_{z}(X_{1}),\ldots,h_{z}(X_{n}). By the defining optimality inequality for KRR,

‖h¯n,z−hz‖n2+λn​‖h¯n,z‖ℋν2≤λn​‖hz‖ℋν2,\|\bar{h}_{n,z}-h_{z}\|_{n}^{2}+\lambda_{n}\|\bar{h}_{n,z}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}^{2}\,\leq\,\lambda_{n}\|h_{z}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}^{2}, (41)

and hence ‖h¯n,z−hz‖n≤λn1/2​‖hz‖ℋν, and ​‖h¯n,z−hz‖ℋν≤2​‖hz‖ℋν.\|\bar{h}_{n,z}-h_{z}\|_{n}\leq\lambda_{n}^{1/2}\|h_{z}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}},\text{ and }\|\bar{h}_{n,z}-h_{z}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}\leq 2\|h_{z}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}. Since tnn−s/d=o(λn1/2)t_{n}n^{-s/d}=o(\lambda_{n}^{1/2}), the definition of ℰn​(tn)\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}) and the norm equivalence between Hs​(𝒳)H^{s}(\mathcal{X}) and ℋν\mathcal{H}_{\nu} imply, on ℰn​(tn)\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}),

‖h¯n,z−hz‖L2≤C​λn1/2​‖hz‖ℋν.\|\bar{h}_{n,z}-h_{z}\|_{L^{2}}\,\leq\,C\lambda_{n}^{1/2}\|h_{z}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}.

Applying the Sobolev interpolation inequality and Equation (40), we obtain the following bound for Bn,zB_{n,z} on ℰn​(tn)\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}):

‖h¯n,z−hz‖∞≤C​‖h¯n,z−hz‖L21−d2​s​‖h¯n,z−hz‖Hsd2​s≤C​λn12−d4​s​‖hz‖ℋν≤C​λn12−d4​s.\displaystyle\|\bar{h}_{n,z}-h_{z}\|_{\infty}\,\leq\,C\|\bar{h}_{n,z}-h_{z}\|_{L^{2}}^{1-\frac{d}{2s}}\|\bar{h}_{n,z}-h_{z}\|_{H^{s}}^{\frac{d}{2s}}\,\leq\,C\lambda_{n}^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d}{4s}}\|h_{z}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\nu}}\,\leq\,C\lambda_{n}^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d}{4s}}. (42)

where CC is independent of zz.

We now compare Sn,zS_{n,z} and Bn,zB_{n,z}. Since λn≍(log⁡n)/n\lambda_{n}\asymp(\log n)/n, we know

λn12−d4​s≍(log⁡nn)12−d4​sandn−1/2λn−d4​slog⁡n≍(log⁡nn)12−d4​s.\lambda_{n}^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d}{4s}}\,\asymp\,\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d}{4s}}\quad\text{and}\quad n^{-1/2}\lambda_{n}^{-\frac{d}{4s}}\sqrt{\log n}\,\asymp\,\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d}{4s}}.

Furthermore, because s=ν+d/2s=\nu+d/2, we have

12−d4​s=ν2​ν+d.\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d}{4s}\,=\,\frac{\nu}{2\nu+d}. (43)

It follows from Equations (42), (22), (20) and (43) that, for every realization of X1:nX_{1:n} belonging to ℰn​(tn)\mathcal{E}_{n}(t_{n}),

ℙ(‖h^n(z;⋅)−hz‖∞>CA(log⁡nn)ν2​ν+d|X1:n)≤12n−A.\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|\hat{h}_{n}(z;\cdot)-h_{z}\right\|_{\infty}>C_{A}\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\frac{\nu}{2\nu+d}}\,\middle|\,X_{1:n}\right)\,\leq\,\frac{1}{2}n^{-A}. (44)

Combining Equation (44) with the design-event probability bound (21) yields

ℙ𝒟n​(‖h^n​(z,⋅)−hz‖∞>CA​(log⁡nn)ν2​ν+d)≤n−A.\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{D}_{n}}\left(\left\|\hat{h}_{n}(z;\cdot)-h_{z}\right\|_{\infty}>C_{A}\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\frac{\nu}{2\nu+d}}\right)\,\leq\,n^{-A}. (45)

Recalling that d=dxd=d_{x}, Equation (45) is exactly Equation (39). All constants above depend only on AA, MM, the uniform Sobolev bound in Assumption 3.2, the density bounds in Assumption 2, and the kernel and domain parameters, and therefore can be chosen independently of zz. This completes the proof. □\square

Lemma 8.4 establishes a high-probability sup-norm error bound for the estimated objective function at each fixed z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, with constants independent of zz. To control the supremum over 𝒵\mathcal{Z} in Equation (18), we need to establish a bound that holds simultaneously for all z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}. We therefore use a covering-number argument to extend the fixed-decision result and obtain the expected uniform approximation error in Lemma 8.6.

Lemma 8.6 (Uniform approximation error for KRR)

Suppose the conditions of Proposition 3.1 hold. Then, the KRR-weighted objective h^n\hat{h}_{n} in Equation (4) satisfies

𝔼𝒟n,X​[supz∈𝒵|h^n​(z,X)−h⁡(z,X)|]=𝒪⁡(n−ν2​ν+dx​log⁡n).\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{n},X}\left[\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\Big|\hat{h}_{n}(z;X)-h(z;X)\Big|\right]=\mathcal{O}\left(n^{-\frac{\nu}{2\nu+d_{x}}}\sqrt{\log n}\right). (46)
Proof 8.7

Proof of Lemma 8.6

Fix ε>0\varepsilon>0. By the compactness of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} in Assumption 2, there exists an ε\varepsilon-net Vε⊂𝒵V_{\varepsilon}\subset\mathcal{Z} with |Vε|≤C​ε−dz|V_{\varepsilon}|\leq C\varepsilon^{-d_{z}} for all sufficiently small ε\varepsilon, where CC is independent of ε\varepsilon (Chapter 4.2 of Vershynin 2018). For any z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, choose v∈Vεv\in V_{\varepsilon} such that ‖z−v‖≤ε\|z-v\|\leq\varepsilon. By the uniform Lipschitz condition in Assumption 2, we have |hz​(x)−hv​(x)|≤G​ε|h_{z}(x)-h_{v}(x)|\leq G\varepsilon for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}. Moreover, by Equation (4),

|h^n​(z,x)−h^n​(v,x)|=|∑i=1nωn,iKRR​(x)​{c⁡(z,Xi,Yi)−c⁡(v,Xi,Yi)}|≤G​ε​∑i=1n|ωn,iKRR​(x)|.|\hat{h}_{n}(z;x)-\hat{h}_{n}(v;x)|\,=\,\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{n,i}^{\rm KRR}(x)\big\{c(z;X_{i},Y_{i})-c(v;X_{i},Y_{i})\big\}\right|\,\leq\,G\varepsilon\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\omega_{n,i}^{\rm KRR}(x)|.

We next bound the ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm of the KRR weights. Since Kn⪰0K_{n}\succeq 0 and λn>0\lambda_{n}>0, we have ‖(Kn+n​λn​In)−1‖op≤(n​λn)−1\|(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\leq(n\lambda_{n})^{-1}, where ‖A‖op:=sup‖u‖2=1‖A​u‖2\|A\|_{\rm op}:=\sup_{\|u\|_{2}=1}\|Au\|_{2} denotes the operator norm induced by the Euclidean norm. Moreover, the boundedness of KνK_{\nu} on 𝒳\mathcal{X} implies supx∈𝒳‖kn​(x)‖2≤C​n\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\|k_{n}(x)\|_{2}\leq C\sqrt{n}. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we have ∑i=1n|ωn,iKRR​(x)|≤n​‖ωKRR​(x)‖2.\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\omega_{n,i}^{\rm KRR}(x)|\leq\sqrt{n}\|\omega^{\rm KRR}(x)\|_{2}. Using the closed-form representation of the KRR weights and the definition of the operator norm, we obtain

supx∈𝒳∑i=1n|ωn,iKRR​(x)|\displaystyle\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\omega_{n,i}^{\rm KRR}(x)| ≤n​supx∈𝒳‖ωKRR​(x)‖2=n​supx∈𝒳‖(Kn+n​λn​In)−1​kn​(x)‖2\displaystyle\leq\,\sqrt{n}\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\|\omega^{\rm KRR}(x)\|_{2}\,=\,\sqrt{n}\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\|(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}k_{n}(x)\|_{2}
≤n​‖(Kn+n​λn​In)−1‖op​supx∈𝒳‖kn​(x)‖2≤n⋅1n​λn⋅C​n=Cλn.\displaystyle\leq\,\sqrt{n}\|(K_{n}+n\lambda_{n}I_{n})^{-1}\|_{\rm op}\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\|k_{n}(x)\|_{2}\,\leq\,\sqrt{n}\cdot\frac{1}{n\lambda_{n}}\cdot C\sqrt{n}\,=\,\frac{C}{\lambda_{n}}.

For any z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, choose v∈Vεv\in V_{\varepsilon} such that ‖z−v‖≤ε\|z-v\|\leq\varepsilon. By the triangle inequality and the preceding bounds, for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

|h^n​(z,x)−hz​(x)|\displaystyle|\hat{h}_{n}(z;x)-h_{z}(x)| ≤|h^n​(v,x)−hv​(x)|+|h^n​(z,x)−h^n​(v,x)|+|hv​(x)−hz​(x)|\displaystyle\leq\,|\hat{h}_{n}(v;x)-h_{v}(x)|+|\hat{h}_{n}(z;x)-\hat{h}_{n}(v;x)|+|h_{v}(x)-h_{z}(x)|
≤|h^n​(v,x)−hv​(x)|+G​ε​(1+Cλn).\displaystyle\leq\,|\hat{h}_{n}(v;x)-h_{v}(x)|+G\varepsilon\left(1+\frac{C}{\lambda_{n}}\right).

Taking the supremum over x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, we obtain

supz∈𝒵‖h^n​(z,⋅)−hz‖∞≤maxv∈Vε⁡‖h^n​(v,⋅)−hv‖∞+G​ε​(1+Cλn).\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\|\hat{h}_{n}(z;\cdot)-h_{z}\|_{\infty}\,\leq\,\max_{v\in V_{\varepsilon}}\|\hat{h}_{n}(v;\cdot)-h_{v}\|_{\infty}+G\varepsilon\left(1+\frac{C}{\lambda_{n}}\right). (47)

Choose εn=λn​(log⁡n/n)ν2​ν+dx\varepsilon_{n}=\lambda_{n}\left({\log n}/{n}\right)^{\frac{\nu}{2\nu+d_{x}}}. We prove Theorem 3.2 by constructing a finite subclass of problem instances in 𝒫β\mathcal{P}_{\beta}. We show that, for any PtO procedure satisfying Assumption 3.3, the expected regret averaged over this subclass is bounded below by a constant multiple of n−4/(dx+4)n^{-4/(d_{x}+4)}. Since the worst-case expected regret over 𝒫β\mathcal{P}_{\beta} is at least this average, the desired lower bound follows.

9.2 Proof of Lemma 4.4

Proof 9.2

Proof. By Assumption 2, we have |c⁡(z,x0,y)|≤M|c(z;x_{0},y)|\leq M for all yy, so a standard characterization of total variation distance (via test functions with bounded range) yields

|h(z;x0)−h¯(z;x0)|≤ 2MTV(FY|X(⋅|x0),F^Y|X(⋅|x0))for all z∈𝒵.\big|h(z;x_{0})-\bar{h}(z;x_{0})\big|\,\leq\,2M\,\mathrm{TV}(F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}),\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}))\quad\text{for all }z\in\mathcal{Z}. (62)

Taking expectations with respect to XX and then with respect to 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} yields

𝔼[𝔼[supz∈𝒵|h(z;X)−h¯(z;X)||𝒟n]]≤ 2M𝔼[𝔼[TV(F^Y|X(⋅|X),FY|X(⋅|X))|𝒟n]].\E\Big[\E\Big[\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}|h(z;X)-\bar{h}(z;X)|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\Big]\Big]\,\leq\,2M\,\E\Big[\E\big[\mathrm{TV}(\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|X),F_{Y|X}(\cdot|X))\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big].

Applying Assumption 4.3.2, we have Equation (12). Therefore, we complete the proof. □\square
