𝔼[𝔼[ℛ(X)|𝒟n]]≤CSAAm−1/2+4MCMn−α0(logn)α1.\E\Big[\E\Big[\mathcal{R}(X)\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\Big]\Big]\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{SAA}}\,m^{-1/2}+4M\,C_{\mathrm{M}}\,n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}.

Setting C:=CSAA+4​M​CMC:=C_{\mathrm{SAA}}+4MC_{\mathrm{M}} gives Equation (15). Therefore, we complete the proof. □\square

9.4 Proof of Remark 4.7

In this section, we prove Equation (16) in Remark 4.7. We continue to use the notations in Section 4. Specifically, we denote FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) as the conditional distribution of YY conditioned on X=xX=x. On the offline stage, we use the historical data 𝒟n={(xi,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{n}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} to learn the conditional distribution or a simulator for Y|{X=x}Y|\{X=x\}, denoted as F^Y|X(⋅|x)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x). On the online stage, when a new covariate X=x0X=x_{0} arrives, we generate mm i.i.d. samples from F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}), denoted as Y^1,Y^2,…,Y^m∼F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{Y}_{1},\hat{Y}_{2},\ldots,\hat{Y}_{m}\sim\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}). Then, we can use SAA to construct a sample objective function h^\hat{h} and solve the simulation-based CSO problem accordingly as

z^n,m∗(x0)∈argminz∈𝒵{h^(z;x0):=1m∑j=1mc(z;x0,Y^j)}.\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0})\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\left\{\hat{h}(z;x_{0}):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}c\big(z;x_{0},\hat{Y}_{j}\big)\right\}. (63)

To isolate the impact of the model error from the SAA error, we define an auxiliary decision rule as

z¯n∗(x0)∈argminz∈𝒵{h¯(z;x0):=𝔼[c(z;X,Y^)|X=x0]},\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0})\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\Big\{\bar{h}(z;x_{0}):=\E\big[c(z;X,\hat{Y})\,|\,X=x_{0}\big]\Big\}, (64)

where Y^∼F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{Y}\sim\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}). Then we have the basic decomposition

‖z^n,m∗​(x0)−z∗​(x0)‖⏟decision error≤‖z^n,m∗​(x0)−z¯n∗​(x0)‖⏟SAA error+‖z¯n∗​(x0)−z∗​(x0)‖⏟model error.\underbrace{\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0})-z^{\ast}(x_{0})\|}_{\text{decision error}}\,\leq\,\underbrace{\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0})-\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0})\|}_{\text{SAA error}}\,+\,\underbrace{\|\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0})-z^{\ast}(x_{0})\|}_{\text{model error}}. (65)

We discuss the SAA error and model error separately, and then summarize their combined impact on the decision error. Throughout this subsection, Assumption 2 remains in force. We additionally impose the following differentiability, smoothness, and strong-convexity conditions.

{assumption}

Suppose that

  1. (a)

    The feasible set 𝒵⊂ℝdz\mathcal{Z}\subset\R^{d_{z}} is nonempty, convex, and compact, with diameter

    diam(𝒵):=sup{∥z1−z2∥:z1,z2∈𝒵}≤D<∞.\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal{Z}):=\sup\big\{\|z_{1}-z_{2}\|:z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathcal{Z}\big\}\leq D<\infty.
  2. (b)

    For every (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, the cost function c⁡(⋅,x,y)c(\cdot;x,y) is continuously differentiable on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and there exists a constant G<∞G<\infty such that for all z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} and all (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y},

    ‖∇zc​(z,x,y)‖≤G.\|\nabla_{z}c(z;x,y)\|\leq G.
  3. (c)

    The cost function c⁡(⋅,x,y)c(\cdot;x,y) is uniformly μ\mu-strongly convex and has uniform LL-Lipschitz gradient on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, i.e., there exist constants μ>0\mu>0 and L≥0L\geq 0 such that for all z1,z2∈𝒵z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathcal{Z} and all (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y},

    c⁡(z2,x,y)−c⁡(z1,x,y)\displaystyle c(z_{2};x,y)-c(z_{1};x,y) ≥∇zc​(z1,x,y)⊤​(z2−z1)+μ2​‖z2−z1‖2,\displaystyle\geq\nabla_{z}c(z_{1};x,y)^{\top}(z_{2}-z_{1})+\frac{\mu}{2}\|z_{2}-z_{1}\|^{2},
    ‖∇zc​(z2,x,y)−∇zc​(z1,x,y)‖\displaystyle\|\nabla_{z}c(z_{2};x,y)-\nabla_{z}c(z_{1};x,y)\| ≤L​‖z2−z1‖.\displaystyle\leq L\|z_{2}-z_{1}\|.

Assumption 9.4(a) is standard in stochastic programming and guarantees that minimizers exist, see, e.g., Shapiro et al. (2009, Chapter 5). Assumptions 9.4(b)–(c) impose uniform smoothness and strong convexity of the cost function with respect to zz, uniformly over (x,y)(x,y); such conditions are routinely used in the analysis of M-estimators and SAA problems to obtain stability and convergence rates for the minimizers; see, e.g., Shapiro et al. (2009, Chapter 5) and van der Vaart (1998, Chapter 5); they are also used in the literature of CSO problem, see, e.g., Hu et al. (2020a), Hu et al. (2020b) and some references in the survey paper Sadana et al. (2025).

9.4.1 The SAA Error.

We analyze the first term in the right-hand side of Equation (65), i.e., the term ‖z^n,m∗​(x0)−z¯n∗​(x0)‖.\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0})-\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0})\|. We fix the covariate value x0x_{0}, and treat the offline data 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} and the learned distribution or simulator F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}) as given. All expectations are taken with respect to the simulation draws Y^1,…,Y^m\hat{Y}_{1},\dots,\hat{Y}_{m} conditional on 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} and X=x0X=x_{0}.

Lemma 9.4

Suppose Assumption 9.4 holds. Fix a covariate value x0x_{0} and a realization of the learned conditional distribution or simulator F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}). Then there exists a constant CSAA<∞C_{\mathrm{SAA}}<\infty, depending only on (μ,L,G,D,dz)(\mu,L,G,D,d_{z}), such that for all m≥2m\geq 2,

𝔼[∥z^n,m∗−z¯n∗∥|𝒟n,X=x0]≤CSAAm−1/2.\E\left[\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}-\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n},X=x_{0}\right]\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{SAA}}\,m^{-1/2}. (66)

Lemma 9.4 shows that, once the simulator F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}) is fixed, the SAA-based decision z^n,m∗\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast} converges to the population decision z¯n∗\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast} at the usual Monte Carlo rate m−1/2m^{-1/2} which reflects the fact that h^\hat{h} is an empirical average of mm i.i.d. samples. In the proof, we bound the gradient error and transfer it to decision error by using the strong monotonicity of the empirical objective’s gradient and the constrained optimality conditions.

Proof 9.5

Proof. We suppress the conditioning on 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} and X=x0X=x_{0} in the notation and write expectations with respect to the simulation draws Y^1,…,Y^m\hat{Y}_{1},\ldots,\hat{Y}_{m}. For brevity, write z¯:=z¯n∗​(x0)\bar{z}:=\bar{z}_{n}^{*}(x_{0}) and z^:=z^n,m∗​(x0)\hat{z}:=\hat{z}_{n,m}^{*}(x_{0}). Assumption 9.4(b)–(c), together with the standing Assumption 2, implies that h¯​(⋅,x0)\bar{h}(\cdot;x_{0}) and h^​(⋅,x0)\hat{h}(\cdot;x_{0}) are differentiable and μ\mu-strongly convex on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Their minimizers are therefore unique. The constrained first-order optimality conditions are

⟨∇h¯​(z¯,x0),z−z¯⟩≥0and⟨∇h^​(z^,x0),z−z^⟩≥0,for ​z∈𝒵.\left\langle\nabla\bar{h}(\bar{z};x_{0}),z-\bar{z}\right\rangle\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\left\langle\nabla\hat{h}(\hat{z};x_{0}),z-\hat{z}\right\rangle\geq 0,\qquad\text{for }z\in\mathcal{Z}.

Let d:=z^−z¯d:=\hat{z}-\bar{z}. Taking z=z^z=\hat{z} in the first inequality and z=z¯z=\bar{z} in the second gives

⟨∇h¯​(z¯,x0),d⟩≥0and⟨∇h^​(z^,x0),d⟩≤0.\left\langle\nabla\bar{h}(\bar{z};x_{0}),d\right\rangle\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\left\langle\nabla\hat{h}(\hat{z};x_{0}),d\right\rangle\leq 0.

Combining with the strong monotonicity of the gradient of the empirical objective h^​(⋅,x0)\hat{h}(\cdot;x_{0}), the above constrained first-order optimality conditions, and Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we have

μ​‖d‖2≤⟨∇h^​(z^,x0)−∇h^​(z¯,x0),d⟩\displaystyle\mu\|d\|^{2}\,\leq\,\left\langle\nabla\hat{h}(\hat{z};x_{0})-\nabla\hat{h}(\bar{z};x_{0}),d\right\rangle
≤\displaystyle\leq −⟨∇h^​(z¯,x0),d⟩≤⟨∇h¯​(z¯,x0)−∇h^​(z¯,x0),d⟩≤‖∇h¯​(z¯,x0)−∇h^​(z¯,x0)‖​‖d‖.\displaystyle-\left\langle\nabla\hat{h}(\bar{z};x_{0}),d\right\rangle\,\leq\,\left\langle\nabla\bar{h}(\bar{z};x_{0})-\nabla\hat{h}(\bar{z};x_{0}),d\right\rangle\,\leq\,\left\|\nabla\bar{h}(\bar{z};x_{0})-\nabla\hat{h}(\bar{z};x_{0})\right\|\|d\|.

If d=0d=0, the desired comparison is immediate. Otherwise, dividing by μ​‖d‖\mu\|d\| yields

‖z^−z¯‖≤1μ​‖∇h^​(z¯,x0)−∇h¯​(z¯,x0)‖.\|\hat{z}-\bar{z}\|\,\leq\,\frac{1}{\mu}\left\|\nabla\hat{h}(\bar{z};x_{0})-\nabla\bar{h}(\bar{z};x_{0})\right\|.

Conditional on 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} and X=x0X=x_{0}, the population minimizer z¯\bar{z} is fixed. Define Vj:=∇zc​(z¯,x0,Y^j)​ and ​a:=𝔼⁡[Vj]=∇h¯​(z¯,x0).V_{j}:=\nabla_{z}c(\bar{z};x_{0},\hat{Y}_{j})\text{ and }a:=\mathbb{E}[V_{j}]=\nabla\bar{h}(\bar{z};x_{0}). The vectors V1,…,VmV_{1},\ldots,V_{m} are i.i.d., and ‖Vj‖≤G\|V_{j}\|\leq G almost surely. Furthermore,

∇h^​(z¯,x0)−∇h¯​(z¯,x0)=1m​∑j=1m(Vj−a).\nabla\hat{h}(\bar{z};x_{0})-\nabla\bar{h}(\bar{z};x_{0})\,=\,\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(V_{j}-a).

For i≠ji\neq j, independence and centering imply 𝔼⁡[⟨Vi−a,Vj−a⟩]=⟨𝔼⁡[Vi−a],𝔼⁡[Vj−a]⟩=0.\mathbb{E}[\langle V_{i}-a,V_{j}-a\rangle]=\langle\mathbb{E}[V_{i}-a],\mathbb{E}[V_{j}-a]\rangle=0. Therefore,

𝔼⁡[‖∇h^​(z¯,x0)−∇h¯​(z¯,x0)‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla\hat{h}(\bar{z};x_{0})-\nabla\bar{h}(\bar{z};x_{0})\right\|^{2}\right]
=\displaystyle= 1m2​∑i=1m∑j=1m𝔼⁡[⟨Vi−a,Vj−a⟩]=1m​𝔼​[‖V1−a‖2]=1m​(𝔼⁡[‖V1‖2]−‖a‖2)≤G2m.\displaystyle\frac{1}{m^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\left[\langle V_{i}-a,V_{j}-a\rangle\right]\,=\,\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{E}\left[\|V_{1}-a\|^{2}\right]\,=\,\frac{1}{m}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\|V_{1}\|^{2}\right]-\|a\|^{2}\right)\,\leq\,\frac{G^{2}}{m}.

Squaring the minimizer comparison and taking expectations gives 𝔼⁡[‖z^−z¯‖2]≤G2μ2​m.\mathbb{E}[\|\hat{z}-\bar{z}\|^{2}]\leq\frac{G^{2}}{\mu^{2}m}. Finally, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality yields

𝔼⁡[‖z^−z¯‖]≤(𝔼⁡[‖z^−z¯‖2])1/2≤Gμ​m.\mathbb{E}\left[\|\hat{z}-\bar{z}\|\right]\leq\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\|\hat{z}-\bar{z}\|^{2}\right]\right)^{1/2}\leq\frac{G}{\mu\sqrt{m}}.

Restoring the conditioning and the original notation proves the claimed bound. Therefore, we complete the proof. □\square

9.4.2 The Model Error.

We now turn to the second term in Equation (65), i.e., the term ‖z¯n∗​(x0)−z∗​(x0)‖\|\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0})-z^{\ast}(x_{0})\|. We begin by quantifying how sensitive the optimal solution is to perturbations of the underlying conditional distribution, measured in total variation distance.

Lemma 9.6

Suppose Assumption 9.4 holds. Fix x0∈𝒳x_{0}\in\mathcal{X} and let ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q} be two probability measures on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. Define

hℙ​(z,x0):=𝔼Y∼ℙ⁡[c⁡(z,x0,Y)],hℚ​(z,x0):=𝔼Y∼ℚ⁡[c⁡(z,x0,Y)],h_{\mathbb{P}}(z;x_{0}):=\E_{Y\sim\mathbb{P}}[c(z;x_{0},Y)],\qquad h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z;x_{0}):=\E_{Y\sim\mathbb{Q}}[c(z;x_{0},Y)],

and let

zℙ∗​(x0):=arg⁡minz∈𝒵​hℙ​(z,x0),zℚ∗​(x0):=arg⁡minz∈𝒵​hℚ​(z,x0).z_{\mathbb{P}}^{\ast}(x_{0}):=\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}h_{\mathbb{P}}(z;x_{0}),\qquad z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\ast}(x_{0}):=\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z;x_{0}).

Then both minimizers are unique, and

‖zℚ∗​(x0)−zℙ∗​(x0)‖≤2​Gμ​TV​(ℚ,ℙ),\big\|z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\ast}(x_{0})-z_{\mathbb{P}}^{\ast}(x_{0})\big\|\;\leq\;\frac{2G}{\mu}\,\mathrm{TV}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{P}), (67)

where TV\mathrm{TV} denotes the total variation distance. In particular, taking ℙ=FY|X(⋅|x0)\mathbb{P}=F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}) and ℚ=F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\mathbb{Q}=\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}) yields

∥z¯n∗(x0)−z∗(x0)∥≤2​GμTV(F^Y|X(⋅|x0),FY|X(⋅|x0)).\big\|\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0})-z^{\ast}(x_{0})\big\|\;\leq\;\frac{2G}{\mu}\,\mathrm{TV}\left(\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}),F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0})\right).

Lemma 9.6 states that the optimal solution is Lipschitz-continuous with respect to the underlying conditional distribution in total variation distance. Intuitively, if we change the distribution of Y|{X=x0}Y|\{X=x_{0}\} only slightly (in total variation), then the expected gradient changes only slightly, and by strong convexity the minimizer cannot move far. This type of stability result is a direct consequence of the standard stability-of-argmin arguments used in M-estimation (see, e.g., van der Vaart 1998, Chapter 5) and in stochastic programming sensitivity analysis (see Shapiro et al. 2009, Chapter 5).

Proof 9.7

Proof. For brevity we write hℙ​(z)h_{\mathbb{P}}(z) and hℚ​(z)h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z) for hℙ​(z,x0)h_{\mathbb{P}}(z;x_{0}) and hℚ​(z,x0)h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z;x_{0}), and zℙ∗z_{\mathbb{P}}^{\ast} and zℚ∗z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\ast} for the corresponding minimizers. By Assumption 9.4(c), for each yy the function z↦c⁡(z,x0,y)z\mapsto c(z;x_{0},y) is μ\mu-strongly convex. Therefore, for any z1,z2∈𝒵z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathcal{Z} and λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1],

c⁡(λ​z1+(1−λ)​z2,x0,y)≤λ​c​(z1,x0,y)+(1−λ)​c​(z2,x0,y)−μ2​λ​(1−λ)​‖z1−z2‖2.c(\lambda z_{1}+(1-\lambda)z_{2};x_{0},y)\,\leq\,\lambda c(z_{1};x_{0},y)+(1-\lambda)c(z_{2};x_{0},y)-\frac{\mu}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\|z_{1}-z_{2}\|^{2}.

Taking expectations with respect to Y∼ℙY\sim\mathbb{P}, we obtain

hℙ​(λ​z1+(1−λ)​z2)≤λ​hℙ​(z1)+(1−λ)​hℙ​(z2)−μ2​λ​(1−λ)​‖z1−z2‖2,h_{\mathbb{P}}(\lambda z_{1}+(1-\lambda)z_{2})\,\leq\,\lambda h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{1})+(1-\lambda)h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{2})-\frac{\mu}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\|z_{1}-z_{2}\|^{2},

so hℙh_{\mathbb{P}} is μ\mu-strongly convex. Similarly hℚh_{\mathbb{Q}} is μ\mu-strongly convex. Hence both have unique minimizers zℙ∗z_{\mathbb{P}}^{\ast} and zℚ∗z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{\ast}. Because hℙh_{\mathbb{P}} and hℚh_{\mathbb{Q}} are differentiable and convex, their constrained minimizers satisfy the variational inequalities

⟨∇hℙ​(zℙ∗),z−zℙ∗⟩≥0and⟨∇hℚ​(zℚ∗),z−zℚ∗⟩≥0,for all ​z∈𝒵.\big\langle\nabla h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}),z-z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}\big\rangle\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\big\langle\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}),z-z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}\big\rangle\geq 0,\qquad\text{for all }z\in\mathcal{Z}.

Taking z=zℚ∗z=z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*} in the first inequality and z=zℙ∗z=z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*} in the second gives

⟨∇hℙ​(zℙ∗),zℚ∗−zℙ∗⟩≥0and⟨∇hℚ​(zℚ∗),zℚ∗−zℙ∗⟩≤0.\big\langle\nabla h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}),z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}-z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}\big\rangle\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\big\langle\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}),z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}-z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}\big\rangle\leq 0.

Let d:=zℚ∗−zℙ∗d:=z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}-z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}. Combining with the strong monotonicity of the gradient of the expected objective hℚh_{\mathbb{Q}}, the above constrained first-order optimality conditions, and Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we have

μ​‖d‖2\displaystyle\mu\|d\|^{2} ≤⟨∇hℚ​(zℚ∗)−∇hℚ​(zℙ∗),d⟩≤−⟨∇hℚ​(zℙ∗),d⟩=⟨∇hℙ​(zℙ∗)−∇hℚ​(zℙ∗),d⟩−⟨∇hℙ​(zℙ∗),d⟩\displaystyle\leq\,\big\langle\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*})-\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}),d\big\rangle\,\leq\,-\big\langle\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}),d\big\rangle\,=\,\big\langle\nabla h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})-\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}),d\big\rangle-\big\langle\nabla h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}),d\big\rangle
≤⟨∇hℙ​(zℙ∗)−∇hℚ​(zℙ∗),d⟩≤‖∇hℙ​(zℙ∗)−∇hℚ​(zℙ∗)‖​‖d‖.\displaystyle\leq\,\big\langle\nabla h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})-\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}),d\big\rangle\,\leq\,\big\|\nabla h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})-\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})\big\|\|d\|.

If d=0d=0, the desired comparison is immediate. Otherwise, dividing by μ​‖d‖\mu\|d\| yields

‖zℚ∗−zℙ∗‖≤1μ​‖∇hℚ​(zℙ∗)−∇hℙ​(zℙ∗)‖.\|z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}-z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}\|\,\leq\,\frac{1}{\mu}\left\|\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})-\nabla h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})\right\|. (68)

By the definitions of hℙh_{\mathbb{P}} and hℚh_{\mathbb{Q}}, we have

∇hℚ​(zℙ∗)−∇hℙ​(zℙ∗)=𝔼Y∼ℚ​[∇zc​(zℙ∗,x0,Y)]−𝔼Y∼ℙ​[∇zc​(zℙ∗,x0,Y)].\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})-\nabla h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})\,=\,\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim\mathbb{Q}}\left[\nabla_{z}c(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*};x_{0},Y)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim\mathbb{P}}\left[\nabla_{z}c(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*};x_{0},Y)\right].

For completeness, if a measurable vector-valued function ff satisfies supy‖f⁡(y)‖≤B\sup_{y}\|f(y)\|\leq B, then

‖𝔼ℚ​[f⁡(Y)]−𝔼ℙ​[f⁡(Y)]‖=sup‖u‖≤1|𝔼ℚ​[u⊤​f​(Y)]−𝔼ℙ​[u⊤​f​(Y)]|≤ 2​B​TV⁡(ℚ,ℙ).\left\|\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[f(Y)]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[f(Y)]\right\|\,=\,\sup_{\|u\|\leq 1}\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[u^{\top}f(Y)]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[u^{\top}f(Y)]\right|\,\leq\,2B\,\operatorname{TV}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{P}).

Applying this inequality with f⁡(y)=∇zc​(zℙ∗,x0,y)f(y)=\nabla_{z}c(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*};x_{0},y) and using Assumption 9.4(b) gives

‖∇hℚ​(zℙ∗)−∇hℙ​(zℙ∗)‖≤ 2​G​TV⁡(ℚ,ℙ).\left\|\nabla h_{\mathbb{Q}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})-\nabla h_{\mathbb{P}}(z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*})\right\|\,\leq\,2G\,\operatorname{TV}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{P}).

Combining this bound with Equation (68) yields

‖zℚ∗−zℙ∗‖≤2​Gμ​TV⁡(ℚ,ℙ),\|z_{\mathbb{Q}}^{*}-z_{\mathbb{P}}^{*}\|\,\leq\,\frac{2G}{\mu}\operatorname{TV}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{P}),

which proves Equation (67). Taking ℙ=FY|X(⋅|x0)\mathbb{P}=F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}) and ℚ=F^Y|X(⋅|x0)\mathbb{Q}=\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x_{0}) gives the stated specialization. Therefore, we complete the proof. □\square

To turn Lemma 9.6 into a quantitative bound on the average model error, we assume that the learned distribution or simulator is consistent in total variation on average over the covariate distribution.

Lemma 9.8

Suppose Assumptions 9.4 and 4.3.2 hold. Then

𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[‖z¯n∗​(X)−z∗​(X)‖|𝒟n]]≤2​Gμ​CM​n−α0​(log⁡n)α1,\E\Big[\E\big[\|\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(X)-z^{\ast}(X)\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big]\;\leq\;\frac{2G}{\mu}\,C_{\mathrm{M}}\,n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}, (69)

where the inner expectation is with respect to XX and the outer expectation is with respect to 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}.

Lemma 9.8 shows that, under the stability result of Lemma 9.6 and the average total variation convergence of Assumption 4.3.2, the decision error due purely to model misspecification (i.e., using F^Y|X(⋅|x)\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) instead of FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x)) decays at the same rate as the simulator itself in total variation. The constant is inflated by the inverse strong-convexity modulus μ−1\mu^{-1} and the gradient envelope GG, reflecting the sensitivity of the optimization problem to perturbations in the objective.

Proof 9.9

Proof. By Lemma 9.6 applied pointwise in xx and taking ℙ=FY|X(⋅|x)\mathbb{P}=F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) and ℚ=F^Y|X(⋅|x)\mathbb{Q}=\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x), we have for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

∥z¯n∗(x)−z∗(x)∥≤2​GμTV(F^Y|X(⋅|x),FY|X(⋅|x)).\|\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x)-z^{\ast}(x)\|\;\leq\;\frac{2G}{\mu}\,\mathrm{TV}\big(\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|x),F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x)\big).

Taking expectations with respect to XX and then with respect to 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} yields

𝔼[𝔼[∥z¯n∗(X)−z∗(X)∥|𝒟n]]≤2​Gμ𝔼[𝔼[TV(F^Y|X(⋅|X),FY|X(⋅|X))|𝒟n]].\E\Big[\E\big[\|\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(X)-z^{\ast}(X)\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big]\,\leq\,\frac{2G}{\mu}\,\E\Big[\E\big[\mathrm{TV}(\hat{F}_{Y|X}(\cdot|X),F_{Y|X}(\cdot|X))\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big].

Applying Assumption 4.3.2 to the right-hand side gives Equation (69), and we complete the proof. □\square

9.4.3 Decision Error Bound for GtO.

We now combine the SAA error bound (Lemma 9.4) and the model error bound (Lemma 9.8) to obtain an overall bound on the decision error of the GtO procedure. Recall the decomposition (65) for a fixed x0x_{0}:

‖z^n,m∗​(x0)−z∗​(x0)‖≤‖z^n,m∗​(x0)−z¯n∗​(x0)‖+‖z¯n∗​(x0)−z∗​(x0)‖.\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0})-z^{\ast}(x_{0})\|\,\leq\,\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(x_{0})-\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0})\|+\|\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(x_{0})-z^{\ast}(x_{0})\|.

We now integrate this bound over the randomness in both the training data and the online covariate, and plug in the bounds obtained in the previous subsections.

Theorem 9.10

Suppose Assumptions 9.4 and 4.3.2 hold. Then there exists a constant C<∞C<\infty, depending only on (μ,L,G,σ,D,dz,CM,α0,α1)(\mu,L,G,\sigma,D,d_{z},C_{\mathrm{M}},\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1}), such that for all integers n,m≥2n,m\geq 2,

𝔼[𝔼[∥z^n,m∗(X)−z∗(X)∥|𝒟n]]≤C(n−α0(logn)α1+m−1/2),\E\Big[\E\big[\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(X)-z^{\ast}(X)\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big]\;\leq\;C\left(n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}+m^{-1/2}\right), (70)

where, conditional on 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}, the inner expectation is with respect to the online covariate XX and the conditional simulation draws, and the outer expectation is with respect to 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}.

Theorem 9.10 provides a clean decomposition of the average decision error of the GtO procedure into: an offline learning error term, n−α0​(log⁡n)α1n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}, which reflects how accurately the conditional distribution FY|X(⋅|x)F_{Y|X}(\cdot|x) can be learned from nn samples, and an online SAA error term, m−1/2m^{-1/2}, which reflects the Monte Carlo error from using mm simulated samples at decision time. In settings where α0=1/2\alpha_{0}=1/2, this yields the canonical rate

𝔼[𝔼[∥z^n,m∗(X)−z∗(X)∥|𝒟n]]=𝒪(n−1/2(logn)α1+m−1/2)=𝒪~(n−1/2+m−1/2).\E\Big[\E\big[\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(X)-z^{\ast}(X)\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big]\,=\,\mathcal{O}\Big(n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}+m^{-1/2}\Big)\,=\,\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\Big(n^{-1/2}+m^{-1/2}\Big).

Theorem 9.10 makes explicit the trade-off between investing in more training data (larger nn) and using more simulation at decision time (larger mm). In particular, if one balances the two error terms by choosing mm as a suitable function of nn, the overall decision error can be minimized.

Proof 9.11

Proof. Taking expectations with respect to XX and then with respect to 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} to the result in Lemma 9.4 yields

𝔼[𝔼[∥z^n,m∗(X)−z¯n∗(X)∥|𝒟n]]≤CSAAm−1/2.\E\Big[\E\big[\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(X)-\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(X)\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big]\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{SAA}}\,m^{-1/2}. (71)

By Lemma 9.8, we have

𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[‖z^n,m∗​(X)−z∗​(X)‖|𝒟n]]\displaystyle\E\Big[\E\big[\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(X)-z^{\ast}(X)\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big] ≤𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[‖z^n,m∗​(X)−z¯n∗​(X)‖|𝒟n]]+𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[‖z¯n∗​(X)−z∗​(X)‖|𝒟n]]\displaystyle\,\leq\,\E\Big[\E\big[\|\hat{z}_{n,m}^{\ast}(X)-\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(X)\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big]+\E\Big[\E\big[\|\bar{z}_{n}^{\ast}(X)-z^{\ast}(X)\|\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}_{n}\big]\Big]
≤CSAAm−1/2+2​GμCMn−α0(logn)α1.\displaystyle\,\leq\,C_{\mathrm{SAA}}\,m^{-1/2}+\frac{2G}{\mu}\,C_{\mathrm{M}}\,n^{-\alpha_{0}}(\log n)^{\alpha_{1}}.

By setting C:=CSAA+2​Gμ​CM,C:=C_{\mathrm{SAA}}+\frac{2G}{\mu}C_{\mathrm{M}}, we can rewrite the above bound and obtain Equation (70). Therefore, we complete the proof. □\square

10 Numerical Study: Implementation and Supplementary Results

This section provides implementation details and supplementary results for Section 6.

10.1 Contextual Newsvendor Problem

10.1.1 Demand and Shortage-Cost Construction.

Conditional demand follows a three-component Gaussian mixture representing low, regular, and high demand states. We divide the covariates into three groups according to their roles in the demand model. Seasonal factors are generated from a uniform distribution and transformed smoothly to determine the component means. Market and operational factors, such as traffic, discounts, and promotions, follow a lognormal distribution and determine the mixture probabilities. Risk-related factors, such as weather and recent demand history, follow a zero-mean multivariate normal distribution and determine the component variances. Given X=x0X=x_{0}, demand is drawn from the resulting mixture and censored at zero. Across covariate dimensions, the parameters are calibrated to keep average demand and the signal-to-noise ratio comparable.

The shortage penalty reflects differences in service priorities and operating conditions. Let xriskx_{\mathrm{risk}} denote the risk-related covariates and define the priority score s⁡(x)=γ⊤​xrisks(x)=\gamma^{\top}x_{\mathrm{risk}}, with γ\gamma normalized so that s⁡(X)s(X) is standard normal. We partition the score into 11 equal-probability intervals using τk=Φ−1​(k/11)\tau_{k}=\Phi^{-1}(k/11) for k=1,…,10k=1,\ldots,10, where Φ\Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Assigning increasing penalty levels from 30 to 120 gives

b⁡(x)={b1,s⁡(x)<τ1,bk,τk−1≤s(x)<τk,k=2,…,10,b11,s⁡(x)≥τ10.b(x)=\begin{cases}b_{1},&s(x)<\tau_{1},\\ b_{k},&\tau_{k-1}\leq s(x)<\tau_{k},\quad k=2,\ldots,10,\\ b_{11},&s(x)\geq\tau_{10}.\end{cases}

The penalty range produces different newsvendor critical fractiles. Because b⁡(x)b(x) is a step function, the conditional objective can be discontinuous in xx even though the conditional demand model varies smoothly.

We consider n∈{800,2000,5000,10000,20000,30000}n\in\{800,2000,5000,10000,20000,30000\} and dx∈{3,6,10,20,40,60,100}d_{x}\in\{3,6,10,20,40,60,100\}. Each setting is evaluated on 100 test contexts over 30 independent replications. Direct PtO estimates the conditional objective, including the context-dependent penalty. Structure-aware PtO instead estimates h+​(z,x)=𝔼⁡[(z−Y)+|X=x]h_{+}(z;x)=\mathbb{E}[(z-Y)^{+}|X=x] and h−​(z,x)=𝔼⁡[(Y−z)+|X=x]h_{-}(z;x)=\mathbb{E}[(Y-z)^{+}|X=x] using the same prediction weights, and combines them as ch​h^+,n​(z,x0)+b⁡(x0)​h^−,n​(z,x0)c_{h}\hat{h}_{+,n}(z;x_{0})+b(x_{0})\hat{h}_{-,n}(z;x_{0}). This formulation incorporates the known penalty directly rather than estimating its discontinuities.

The empirical objective is piecewise linear in the one-dimensional order quantity. We optimize it by evaluating demand breakpoints. This approach also accommodates signed weights when the objective is bounded below. On the unrestricted domain z≥0z\geq 0, the terminal slope must be nonnegative, and the feasible endpoint z=0z=0 must be included among the candidates. Thus, efficient optimization in this setting does not require convexity.

10.1.2 Detailed Performance and Online Time.

Tables 10.1.2 and 10.1.2 report the method-level relative costs for the direct and structure-aware formulations, respectively, corresponding to Panels (a) and (b) of Figure 6.2.2. Higher relative cost indicates better decision performance. The GtO results are identical across the two tables; the PtO columns report the respective formulations.

Tables 10.1.2 and 10.1.2 report online times for the two formulations. PtO generally requires hundredths of a second, whereas GtO takes approximately 0.49 to 6.57 seconds across the tested settings. At n=10,000n=10{,}000, structure-aware PtO takes approximately 0.013 to 0.042 seconds and GtO takes 0.76 to 2.80 seconds. These are the entries summarized in Table 6.2.2 in the main text.

10.2 Product Placement Problem

10.2.1 Network and Demand Construction.

A retailer operates dyd_{y} stores connected by a directed transportation network G=(V,𝒜)G=(V,\mathcal{A}), where |V|=dy|V|=d_{y}. After observing X=x0X=x_{0}, the retailer chooses initial inventory z∈ℝ+dyz\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d_{y}} at cost α⊤​z\alpha^{\top}z. Once demand Y∈ℝ+dyY\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d_{y}} is realized, inventory can be transferred between stores. Let f∈ℝ+|𝒜|f\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{|\mathcal{A}|} denote transfers and p∈ℝ+dyp\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d_{y}} unmet demand. The incidence matrix A∈ℝdy×|𝒜|A\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}\times|\mathcal{A}|} has entries 1 at an arc’s origin and −1-1 at its destination, so A​fAf is net outflow and z−A​fz-Af is inventory after transfers.

Given zz and demand yy, the recourse problem minimizes transportation and shortage costs:

Q(z,y)=minf,p{g⊤f+r⊤p:z−Af+p≥y,f≥0,p≥0},Q(z,y)=\min_{f,p}\left\{g^{\top}f+r^{\top}p:\ z-Af+p\geq y,\ f\geq 0,\ p\geq 0\right\},

where g∈ℝ+|𝒜|g\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{|\mathcal{A}|} and r∈ℝ+dyr\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d_{y}} are unit transportation and shortage costs. The initial placement decision minimizes α⊤​z+𝔼⁡[Q⁡(z,Y)|X=x0]\alpha^{\top}z+\mathbb{E}[Q(z,Y)|X=x_{0}] over 0≤z≤U0\leq z\leq U, where U∈ℝ+dyU\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d_{y}} specifies store-level inventory upper bounds.

We extend the newsvendor’s three-component Gaussian mixture to multivariate demand. Each store has the same marginal model specification, with dependence introduced so that stores closer in the network have stronger demand correlations. Demand is censored at zero coordinatewise. The network contains 2​dy2d_{y} directed arcs: dyd_{y} form a ring, and the remaining dyd_{y} are generated randomly once per replication. We fix dx=10d_{x}=10 and n=104n=10^{4} and vary dy∈{1,2,5,10,15}d_{y}\in\{1,2,5,10,15\}. Average demand and marginal variability at each store are calibrated to remain comparable across dimensions. Unit placement, transportation, and shortage costs are 2, 1, and 10, respectively.

10.2.2 Optimization with Nonnegative and Signed Weights.

The weighted problem minimizes α⊤​z+∑s=1Sωs​Q​(z,ys)\alpha^{\top}z+\sum_{s=1}^{S}\omega_{s}Q(z,y^{s}) over 0≤z≤U0\leq z\leq U, where ysy^{s} are observed or generated demand scenarios and ωs\omega_{s} their weights. With nonnegative weights, the scenario recourse problems can be incorporated into the outer minimization, yielding the linear program

minz,{fs,ps}s=1S\displaystyle\min_{z,\{f^{s},p^{s}\}_{s=1}^{S}} α⊤​z+∑s=1Sωs​(g⊤​fs+r⊤​ps)\displaystyle\alpha^{\top}z+\sum_{s=1}^{S}\omega_{s}\left(g^{\top}f^{s}+r^{\top}p^{s}\right)
s.t.\displaystyle\mathrm{s.t.} z−Afs+ps≥ys,s=1,…,S,\displaystyle z-Af^{s}+p^{s}\geq y^{s},\quad s=1,\ldots,S,
0≤z≤U,\displaystyle 0\leq z\leq U,
fs≥0,ps≥0,s=1,…,S.\displaystyle f^{s}\geq 0,\quad p^{s}\geq 0,\quad s=1,\ldots,S.

This formulation applies to SAA, nonnegative-weight PtO methods, and GtO, which assigns equal weights to generated scenarios.

Signed KRR weights require a different treatment. The recourse problem has the dual representation Q⁡(z,y)=maxλ∈Λ⁡(y−z)⊤​λQ(z,y)=\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(y-z)^{\top}\lambda, where Λ={λ:−A⊤λ≤g, 0≤λ≤r}\Lambda=\{\lambda:-A^{\top}\lambda\leq g,\ 0\leq\lambda\leq r\}. For ωs<0\omega_{s}<0, this implies ωs​Q​(z,ys)=minλs∈Λ⁡ωs​(ys−z)⊤​λs\omega_{s}Q(z,y^{s})=\min_{\lambda^{s}\in\Lambda}\omega_{s}(y^{s}-z)^{\top}\lambda^{s}. Define 𝒮+={s:ωs≥0}\mathcal{S}_{+}=\{s:\omega_{s}\geq 0\} and 𝒮−={s:ωs<0}\mathcal{S}_{-}=\{s:\omega_{s}<0\}. Using the primal representation for nonnegative weights and the dual representation for negative weights gives

minz,{fs,ps}s∈𝒮+,{λs}s∈𝒮−α⊤​z+∑s∈𝒮+ωs​(g⊤​fs+r⊤​ps)+∑s∈𝒮−ωs​(ys−z)⊤​λss.t.z−A​fs+ps≥ys,s∈𝒮+,fs≥0,ps≥0,s∈𝒮+,−A⊤​λs≤g,s∈𝒮−,0≤λs≤r,s∈𝒮−,0≤z≤U.{\begin{array}[]{r@{\quad}l@{\quad}l}\displaystyle\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}z,\{f^{s},p^{s}\}_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{+}},\\ \{\lambda^{s}\}_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{-}}\end{subarray}}&\lx@intercol\displaystyle\alpha^{\top}z+\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{+}}\omega_{s}\left(g^{\top}f^{s}+r^{\top}p^{s}\right)+\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{-}}\omega_{s}(y^{s}-z)^{\top}\lambda^{s}\hfil\lx@intercol\\ \mathrm{s.t.}&z-Af^{s}+p^{s}\geq y^{s},&s\in\mathcal{S}_{+},\\ &f^{s}\geq 0,\quad p^{s}\geq 0,&s\in\mathcal{S}_{+},\\ &-A^{\top}\lambda^{s}\leq g,&s\in\mathcal{S}_{-},\\ &0\leq\lambda^{s}\leq r,&s\in\mathcal{S}_{-},\\ &0\leq z\leq U.&\end{array}} (PP-KRR)

When 𝒮−\mathcal{S}_{-} is empty, (PP-KRR) reduces to (PP-LP). Otherwise, the products −ωs​z⊤​λs-\omega_{s}z^{\top}\lambda^{s} introduce bilinear terms, producing a generally nonconvex formulation. Gurobi’s global optimization procedure can address this formulation, but may become computationally expensive as the number of scenarios and decision dimension increase.

We instead exploit the difference-of-convex decomposition

α⊤​z+∑s=1Sωs​Q​(z,ys)=α⊤​z+∑s∈𝒮+ωs​Q​(z,ys)⏟C⁡(z)−∑s∈𝒮−|ωs|​Q​(z,ys)⏟H⁡(z).\alpha^{\top}z+\sum_{s=1}^{S}\omega_{s}Q(z,y^{s})\,=\,\underbrace{\alpha^{\top}z+\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{+}}\omega_{s}Q(z,y^{s})}_{C(z)}-\underbrace{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{-}}|\omega_{s}|Q(z,y^{s})}_{H(z)}.

Both CC and HH are convex because Q⁡(⋅,ys)Q(\cdot,y^{s}) is convex. At each DCA iteration, we replace −H-H by its affine approximation using a subgradient of HH at the current iterate, then solve the resulting convex subproblem with Gurobi. DCA does not generally certify global optimality, so the reported decision quality and runtime reflect this implementation. Table 6.3.2 in the main paper reports the results for all five demand dimensions.

10.3 Real Case Study: KRR with Categorical Covariates

In the real-case experiment, categorical variables are represented using one-hot encoding, resulting in binary indicators. For KRR, we use the Gaussian kernel

K⁡(x,x′)=exp⁡(−‖x−x′‖2ℓ),K(x,x^{\prime})=\exp(-\frac{\|x-x'\|^2}{\ell}),

where ℓ>0\ell>0 is the kernel bandwidth parameter. Since the Gaussian kernel only depends on the squared Euclidean distance between covariate vectors, binary indicators can be treated in the same way as continuous covariates. Specifically, for each binary indicator xj∈{0,1}x_{j}\in\{0,1\}, its multiplicative contribution to the kernel is

exp⁡(−(xj−xj′)2ℓ)={1,xj=xj′,exp(−1/ℓ),xj≠xj′.\exp\Bigg(-\frac{\big(x_j-x_j'\big)^2}{\ell}\Bigg)\,=\,\begin{cases}1,&x_{j}=x_{j}^{\prime},\\ \exp(-1/\ell),&x_{j}\neq x_{j}^{\prime}.\end{cases}

Thus, matching indicator values leave the kernel similarity unchanged, whereas differing values introduce a discount factor of exp(−1/ℓ)<1\exp(-1/\ell)<1, reducing the similarity between the two observations. Consequently, one-hot-encoded categorical variables can be naturally incorporated into the Gaussian kernel alongside continuous covariates by directly evaluating the kernel on the full covariate vectors xx and x′x^{\prime}.
